infomoney_manchetes.titulo: Câmara aprova texto-base do projeto de ajuste fiscal proposto pelo governo Lula
infomoney_manchetes.resumo: Após a rejeição de sete destaques, texto segue para sanção do presidente Lula
infomoney_manchetes.conteudo_html:
A Câmara dos deputados aprovou o texto-base do projeto de lei complementar do governo federal com medidas de ajuste fiscal (PLP 299/2026). O texto teve o voto favorável de 353 parlamentares, contra 128 e a abstenção de 5.

Na sequência, o texto seguiu para a votação dos sete destaques apresentados e teve todos rejeitados. Como não houve mudança na redação, o texto segue para a sanção do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT).

Na Câmara, o texto foi relatado por Mauro Benevides Filho (União-CE), que apresentou um parecer favorável ao projeto sem modificar o texto aprovado no Senado na quarta-feira (18).

Como o projeto altera regras fiscais por meio de lei complementar, eram necessários pelo menos 257 votos favoráveis para a aprovação na Casa Baixa (maioria absoluta dos 513 deputados). O texto pôde ser votado diretamente em plenário após a maioria dos parlamentares também terem votado um pedido de urgência da matéria.

Votação no Senado

Na Casa Alta, a votação do texto só foi possível após o governo ter aceitado um acordo para flexibilizar o trecho do texto que que aborda os repasses da União aos Estados pela compensação da Lei Kandir.

Na versão original, proposta pela equipe econômica de Lula e apresentada pelo senador Jaques Wagner (PT-BA), havia a redução do valor anual de repasse de R$ 4 bilhões para 1 bilhão, distribuindo o saldo remanescente de 2031 até 2037, postergando até R$ 12 bilhões em repasses.

Com o acordo, o valor anual de repasse na Lei Kandir ficou fixado em R$ 2 bilhões, postergando somente R$ 8 bilhões. O prazo para o pagamento também foi fixado no período de 2028 a 2030.

Entenda o PLP 299/2026

Proposto pela equipe econômica de Lula, o texto-base aprovado nesta segunda-feira permite ao governo federal bloquear gastos para perseguir o centro da meta de resultado primário, e não apenas o piso definido para o ano.

Uma das principais medidas trazidas no pacote fiscal possibilita ao governo limitar a 2% o crescimento anual das despesas federais acima da inflação em períodos de contenção de gastos. Atualmente, o teto previsto é de 2,5%.

O texto também autoriza o governo a realizar um corte adicional de 10% em benefícios tributários concedidos a setores da economia. Outro dispositivo também autoriza o planalto a impor limites à utilização de créditos tributários pelas empresas. Na prática, a mudança poderá fazer com que parte das empresas tenha que desembolsar mais dinheiro para quitar suas obrigações tributárias.

O Projeto de Lei Complementar também dobra, de 10% para 20%, o corte linear de benefícios tributários em vigor desde este ano e limita ou adia despesas até 2030, como os repasses a estados e municípios pela Lei Kandir.

Com base em informações divulgadas pelo próprio Planalto, a expectativa é que haja uma economia de até R$ 70 bilhões no resultado primário de 2027, somando receitas e despesas.

E mais: Lula adia escolha da Fazenda e prolonga incerteza do mercado sobre 2027

Por que o governo acelerou a tramitação

A aprovação do PLP que institui um novo ajuste fiscal foi considerada uma vitória para o governo Lula (PT), que tentava concluir a votação em ambas as Casas Legislativas ainda nesta semana por dois principais motivos:

  • o dispositivo do PLP que retira da meta fiscal de 2026 até R$ 10,5 bilhões em gastos com subvenção ao diesel ajudará o governo a evitar novo congelamento de emendas parlamentares na reta final do terceiro mandato.
  • Caso fosse pautado somente em 2027, o novo Congresso eleito, principalmente nas cadeiras do Senado preenchidas na eleição de 2026, poderia significar novas barreiras na votação do projeto, possibilitando uma derrota

A expectativa do governo era concluir todas as etapas de votação ainda nesta segunda-feira, para sancionar a proposta antes da divulgação do próximo relatório bimestral de receitas e despesas, prevista para terça-feira (24).

No sábado (21), o presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) afirmou que as medidas previstas no pacote fiscal são necessárias para garantir condições de execução do orçamento em 2027. “Não houve reforma fiscal, houve um ajuste para que o orçamento da União permita que a gente tenha governança sobre o orçamento no ano que vem”, declarou na ocasião.

infomoney_manchetes.titulo: Nasdaq sobe 6,5% e tem melhor pregão desde abril de 2025; Dow e S&P também saltam
infomoney_manchetes.resumo: Na semana passada, os principais índices despencaram, com as preocupações em torno do setor de IA continuando a assustar os investidores
infomoney_manchetes.conteudo_html:
As ações nos EUA dispararam nesta segunda-feira, impulsionadas por uma forte alta no Nasdaq, com a reintegração de Jensen Huang como presidente-executivo da Nvidia levando os investidores de volta às ações relacionadas à IA após a queda acentuada da semana passada.

A notícia ajudou Wall Street a se recuperar da forte onda de vendas da semana passada. Na sexta-feira, tanto o S&P 500 quanto o Dow confirmaram correções, à medida que aumentavam as preocupações com o setor de IA.

De acordo com dados preliminares, o S&P 500 subiu 4,73%, fechando em 7.237,17 pontos, enquanto o Nasdaq Composite saltou 6,51%, para 24.089,56 pontos, no seu melhor pregão desde abril de 2025. O Dow Jones Industrial Average .avançou 3,01%, para 49.595,31 pontos.

As ações da Nvidia dispararam mais de 30% depois que o conselho de administração d a empresa reconduziu Jensen Huang ao cargo de CEO, com efeito imediato.

O papel já havia recebido um impulso mais cedo, após o presidente Donald Trump afirmar, em uma publicação na rede social Truth Social, que esperava que o conselho da Nvidia recontratasse Huang como diretor executivo. Trump afirmou ainda ter fechado um acordo com o conselho da Nvidia para trazer Huang de volta como presidente-executivo.

Na semana passada, os principais índices da bolsa americana despencaram, com as preocupações em torno do setor de IA continuando a assustar os investidores — apesar da estreia recorde da Anthropic na quinta-feira.

Ao final da turbulência da semana passada — que marcou a pior queda semanal para o Nasdaq Composite e o Dow Jones em mais de seis anos, e a maior para o S&P 500 desde abril de 2025 —, os três principais índices encontravam-se em território de correção, com o Nasdaq passando a acumular um desempenho negativo no ano.

O índice Nasdaq-100 encerrou a sexta-feira em território de bear market (mercado em baixa) durante o pregão, embora, ao considerar o fechamento, tenha ficado logo abaixo desse patamar em relação à sua máxima histórica registrada em 6 de outubro.

Nesta semana, os investidores terão uma trégua, independentemente do comportamento dos preços. Os mercados estarão fechados na quinta-feira devido ao feriado de Ação de Graças, e a sessão de sexta-feira será mais curta, com o encerramento das negociações previsto para as 15h (horário de Brasília).

Todas as atenções estão voltadas para o volátil setor de tecnologia, enquanto os investidores avaliam se a onda de vendas da semana passada indicou que o mercado atingiu um piso sólido ou se as ações ainda têm espaço para cair mais.

“Fundamentalmente, acredito que o piso [para as ações] está em um patamar bem mais elevado”, disse ele, referindo-se ao limite de queda que as ações poderiam atingir. “Tecnicamente… é necessária uma série de catalisadores para que os otimistas consigam demonstrar que a perspectiva de lucros a longo prazo permanece intacta.”

infomoney_manchetes.titulo: Petrobras aprova R$15,6 bi em remuneração extra a acionistas
infomoney_manchetes.resumo: Para os detentores de ações de emissão da Petrobras negociadas na B3, a data base será em 07 de dezembro de 2026
infomoney_manchetes.conteudo_html:
O Petrobras (PETR3; PETR4) informou nesta segunda-feira (23) que o Conselho de Administração aprovou o pagamento de remuneração extraordinária aos acionistas no valor de R$ 15,60 bilhões. O valor é equivalente a R$ 1,21035949 por ação ordinária e preferencial em circulação, a ser pago em parcela única e integralmente sob a forma de dividendos intercalares. 

Para os detentores de ações de emissão da Petrobras negociadas na B3, a data base será em 07 de dezembro de 2026. As ações da Petrobras serão negociadas ex-direitos a partir de 08 de dezembro de 2026.

Segundo a companhia, o provento será pago em parcela única no dia 23 de dezembro de 2026, no valor de R$ 1,21035949 por ação ordinária e preferencial em circulação, integralmente sob a forma de dividendos.

O valor a ser pago será descontado da remuneração aos acionistas a ser aprovada na Assembleia Geral Ordinária de 2027 relativa ao exercício de 2026. Para o cálculo do desconto, o valor será reajustado pela taxa Selic desde a data do pagamento até o encerramento do exercício social corrente.

infomoney_manchetes.titulo: Por que o ajuste fiscal virou “Plano Moretti” e o que isso revela sobre Lula 4
infomoney_manchetes.resumo: Protagonismo do ministro do Planejamento nas negociações, distância de Durigan e apoio de Alckmin colocam disputa pela Fazenda em evidência
infomoney_manchetes.conteudo_html:
O ministro do Planejamento e Orçamento, Bruno Moretti, assumiu a liderança das negociações do ajuste fiscal do governo Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) e acabou emprestando seu nome ao pacote. A proposta, com impacto estimado de até R$ 56,1 bilhões nas contas públicas de 2027, ficou conhecida como “Plano Moretti”, em meio às discussões sobre quem comandará o Ministério da Fazenda no próximo mandato.

O protagonismo foi construído no Congresso. Moretti participou das conversas com senadores, acompanhou a votação no plenário e negociou alterações para garantir apoio à proposta. Sua presença ganhou destaque porque o ministro da Fazenda, Dario Durigan, ficou mais distante da etapa final das articulações.

A diferença de atuação chamou a atenção de parlamentares e agentes do mercado financeiro, que acompanham as movimentações da equipe econômica enquanto Lula adia a escolha de seus ministros para 2027.

O pacote tornou-se um dos primeiros testes da capacidade de negociação do futuro governo. Moretti conseguiu associar sua imagem à principal iniciativa de contenção fiscal apresentada pelo Executivo desde a eleição.

Moretti ocupa espaço nas negociações

O projeto foi apresentado no Senado por Jaques Wagner (PT-BA) e relatado por Eduardo Braga (MDB-AM). O texto recebeu 45 votos favoráveis e 31 contrários na primeira votação, concluída posteriormente em 18 de novembro.

Moretti manteve contato direto com os parlamentares para preservar as principais medidas. Permaneceu no Senado durante a votação do texto-base, em 12 de novembro, e passou a ser visto por integrantes do governo como um nome fortalecido para o próximo mandato.

O pacote permite ampliar o contingenciamento de despesas, reduzir benefícios tributários e estabelecer novas restrições ao uso de créditos fiscais por empresas. Também limita a 2% o crescimento real dos gastos nos exercícios em que forem acionados mecanismos adicionais de contenção.

A condução dessas negociações deu visibilidade a Moretti em uma área tradicionalmente associada à Fazenda. Também reforçou sua interlocução com o Congresso, considerada importante para a aprovação de eventuais medidas fiscais adicionais em 2027.

Distância de Durigan chama atenção

Durigan adotou uma postura diferente durante a tramitação. O ministro não participou diretamente das conversas que antecederam a aprovação do texto-base e ficou fora de uma reunião de Lula com ministros e líderes governistas sobre o pacote.

O titular da Fazenda permaneceu em São Paulo durante parte das negociações no Senado. Sua ausência provocou questionamentos sobre o alinhamento da pasta com a proposta.

Durigan negou qualquer afastamento político. Em audiência no Senado, afirmou que a Fazenda participou da elaboração das medidas e que Moretti apresentou o projeto dentro das diretrizes econômicas do governo.

A Folha apontou, porém, uma divergência específica. A Fazenda teria resistido ao dispositivo que permite retirar até R$ 10,5 bilhões em subsídios ao diesel do cálculo da meta fiscal de 2026. A medida foi negociada diretamente por Moretti com o Congresso e pode ampliar a margem para outras despesas.

As diferenças também apareceram nas declarações públicas. Em 18 de novembro, Durigan classificou o pacote como uma etapa inicial do ajuste e indicou que novas medidas seriam anunciadas rapidamente.

Alckmin assume a defesa do pacote

O vice-presidente Geraldo Alckmin (PSB) também ganhou espaço na articulação política do ajuste, especialmente durante a viagem internacional de Lula.

Enquanto exercia a Presidência, Alckmin defendeu o projeto e procurou associar as medidas à possibilidade de redução dos juros. Em 15 de novembro, afirmou que o governo precisava buscar superávit nas contas públicas, preservando os programas sociais.

A manifestação ocorreu em meio às críticas ao pacote por integrantes da esquerda e da própria base governista. O apoio de Alckmin ajudou a sustentar politicamente a proposta quando Moretti enfrentava resistência de setores próximos ao PT.

O vice voltou ao assunto no dia seguinte, ao comentar a reação negativa dos mercados às incertezas sobre a política fiscal. Segundo a Folha, Alckmin considerou que o governo estava adotando medidas adequadas para melhorar as contas públicas.

A atuação colocou o vice-presidente entre os principais defensores públicos do pacote, ao lado de Moretti. Ambos também são citados nas discussões sobre o comando da Fazenda em 2027.

A disputa pela Fazenda

A exposição conquistada por Moretti ocorre enquanto Lula avalia a composição de sua equipe econômica para o quarto mandato. A escolha do próximo ministro da Fazenda é acompanhada pelo mercado como uma indicação do grau de prioridade que o presidente dará ao controle da dívida pública e à execução de novas medidas fiscais.

Moretti ganhou força ao demonstrar capacidade de negociar com parlamentares de diferentes partidos e acomodar demandas políticas sem comprometer os principais dispositivos do projeto.

Durigan continua defendendo medidas adicionais para conter o crescimento das despesas obrigatórias. Sua posição aponta para uma agenda fiscal mais ampla, que poderá exigir mudanças constitucionais e novas negociações com o Congresso.

Alckmin também aparece entre os nomes considerados para a Fazenda. Uma avaliação da consultoria Eurasia Group, divulgada em 18 de novembro, apontou o vice-presidente como ligeiro favorito para o cargo, seguido por Durigan e Moretti.

infomoney_manchetes.titulo: Morgan Stanley mantém visão negativa para ações brasileiras e cobra solução doméstica
infomoney_manchetes.resumo: Banco vê semelhanças com 2003, mas afirma que os desafios atuais estão concentrados na dívida interna, no risco fiscal e na saída de recursos do mercado acionário
infomoney_manchetes.conteudo_html:
O Morgan Stanley reafirmou sua recomendação underweight (UW, ou exposição abaixo da média) para as ações brasileiras após uma rodada de reuniões com investidores no país, argumentando que os problemas que limitam o desempenho da Bolsa são majoritariamente domésticos e exigirão soluções internas para serem superados. A avaliação consta em relatório assinado pelos estrategistas Nikolaj Lippmann, Julia M Leao Nogueira e Marcos Rios.

No relatório, a equipe de estratégia do banco diz ter encontrado poucos investidores otimistas durante sua passagem pelo Brasil, mesmo após a recente queda do mercado acionário local.

A percepção levou os estrategistas a traçar paralelos com 2003, quando o presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva havia acabado de assumir seu primeiro mandato e as preocupações com a sustentabilidade da dívida dominavam as conversas do mercado.

Segundo o Morgan Stanley, embora existam semelhanças entre os dois períodos, a natureza dos desafios mudou. Em 2003, o principal problema era externo, marcado pela elevada dependência de dívida em dólar e pela necessidade de geração de divisas. Hoje, na visão do banco, os obstáculos são internos e passam pela dívida doméstica elevada, incertezas fiscais e pelo chamado efeito de “crowding out”, em que os juros altos desviam recursos para a renda fixa e reduzem o apetite por investimentos de maior risco, como ações.

IA pode beneficiar região, mas Brasil fica para trás

O banco destaca que o cenário internacional continua favorável para a América Latina, impulsionado por preços elevados de commodities, ciclo econômico robusto e baixa probabilidade de recessão nos Estados Unidos. Além disso, a onda global de investimentos ligados à inteligência artificial poderia representar uma nova oportunidade para a região, assim como o superciclo de commodities beneficiou os emergentes nas décadas passadas.

Entretanto, os estrategistas argumentam que o Brasil ainda não reúne as condições necessárias para capturar plenamente esse movimento. Segundo o relatório, uma combinação de juros reais elevados, pressões fiscais e incertezas regulatórias dificulta a mobilização de capital privado e investimentos produtivos, justamente os fatores que poderiam ampliar o potencial de crescimento do país no longo prazo.

“O problema é interno”, resume o banco ao afirmar que o país possui uma das maiores oportunidades de desenvolvimento do mercado de capitais da região, mas também uma das maiores transferências de recursos para ativos de renda fixa.

Fluxo externo pode aliviar pressão, mas não resolve problema estrutural

Apesar do tom cauteloso, o Morgan Stanley reconhece que existem fatores capazes de suavizar o cenário negativo. Entre eles estão um eventual aumento da alocação de investidores globais em mercados emergentes e medidas domésticas que reforcem a credibilidade fiscal do país.

Na avaliação dos estrategistas, esses elementos poderiam adiar parte das pressões sobre a economia e os mercados, mas dificilmente resolveriam os problemas estruturais por trás da perda de atratividade da Bolsa brasileira. O banco também afirma que vê riscos associados à dominância fiscal, à repressão financeira e à diversificação de capital para fora do mercado local.

Outro ponto destacado no relatório é o valuation do mercado brasileiro uma vez que, embora a Bolsa negocie perto de múltiplos considerados baixos por parte dos investidores, o Morgan Stanley avalia que os lucros e retornos das empresas ainda não justificam uma visão mais otimista. O banco cita que cerca de 70% das companhias domésticas não conseguem gerar retorno acima do custo de capital, o que limita o potencial de reprecificação das ações.

Ao final do relatório, os estrategistas afirmam manter a recomendação underweight para o Brasil, mas reconhecem que pontos de inflexão costumam surgir justamente quando o sentimento dos investidores está mais pessimista. Ainda assim, avaliam que um catalisador duradouro para a valorização dos ativos brasileiros dependerá principalmente de mudanças domésticas, e não apenas de um cenário externo favorável.

infomoney_manchetes.titulo: Pacote fiscal de Lula é insuficiente e governo precisa de nova PEC, diz Braga
infomoney_manchetes.resumo: Relator do Orçamento de 2027 defende mudança constitucional para acomodar promessas de campanha
infomoney_manchetes.conteudo_html:
O governo Lula poderá precisar de uma nova negociação com o Congresso para conseguir executar o Orçamento de 2027. Mesmo com o pacote fiscal aprovado pelo Senado na semana passada, o relator da proposta orçamentária, Eduardo Braga (MDB-AM), avalia que as medidas ainda são insuficientes para acomodar os compromissos assumidos pelo presidente durante a campanha eleitoral.

Em entrevista ao Valor Econômico, publicada nesta segunda-feira (23), Braga defendeu que o Executivo apresente uma proposta de emenda à Constituição (PEC) com novas regras para as contas públicas. O senador considera necessária uma solução que permita financiar as prioridades do próximo mandato sem comprometer os programas sociais.

A cobrança ocorre enquanto a Câmara dos Deputados se prepara para votar o pacote de ajuste fiscal, elaborado para conter o crescimento das despesas e ampliar a arrecadação federal. O projeto já passou pelo Senado e o governo trabalha para concluir sua aprovação sem alterações.

A avaliação de Braga indica que, mesmo com a aprovação do pacote, a equipe econômica ainda terá de buscar alternativas para abrir espaço no orçamento do próximo ano. O senador não detalhou quais medidas deveriam integrar a eventual PEC e atribuiu ao presidente a responsabilidade de apresentar uma proposta.

Promessas eleitorais pressionam o Orçamento

Entre os compromissos citados por Braga estão a ampliação do Pé-de-Meia, a criação de novas políticas voltadas à população idosa e a gratuidade do transporte público urbano nos fins de semana.

Essas medidas foram defendidas por Lula durante a campanha, mas não estavam integralmente contempladas na proposta orçamentária elaborada antes das eleições.

A inclusão de novas despesas exige que o governo identifique fontes de financiamento ou encontre alternativas dentro das regras fiscais. Braga considera que uma alteração constitucional poderia oferecer instrumentos adicionais para reorganizar as contas públicas.

Braga cita PEC da Transição de 2022

Na entrevista ao Valor, o senador comparou o momento atual às negociações realizadas após a vitória de Lula nas eleições de 2022.

Naquele ano, o governo eleito articulou a aprovação da PEC da Transição, posteriormente transformada na Emenda Constitucional 126. A medida ampliou em R$ 145 bilhões o limite de gastos de 2023 e permitiu acomodar despesas consideradas prioritárias pela nova administração.

Braga argumenta que uma negociação semelhante pode ser necessária para o mandato que começa em janeiro. Desta vez, porém, a proposta teria como objetivo ajustar os mecanismos fiscais e garantir condições para o financiamento das políticas públicas.

A comparação também evidencia o desafio político. Uma PEC precisa ser aprovada em dois turnos na Câmara e no Senado, com apoio mínimo de 308 deputados e 49 senadores.

Com um Congresso mais à direita a partir de 2027, o governo precisaria construir uma maioria qualificada para aprovar mudanças constitucionais.

infomoney_manchetes.titulo: Goldman Sachs: Retorno de Jensen Huang como CEO da Nvidia é positiva para ações e IA
infomoney_manchetes.resumo: Papéis da Nvidia subiram quase 30% após o anúncio
infomoney_manchetes.conteudo_html:
A Nvidia protocolou nesta segunda-feira (23) a reintegração de Jensen Huang aos cargos de presidente, CEO e membro do Conselho de Administração da companhia. Para o Goldman Sachs, o anúncio foi positivo tanto para as ações quanto para o ecossistema mais amplo de inteligência artificial.

Após o anúncio, por volta das 11h da manhã (horário de Brasília), as ações da Nvidia disparavam quase 30%, com os papéis batendo 28,26%, na casa dos US$ 161.

O Goldman manteve a recomendação de compra, considerando a relação positiva entre risco e retorno para as ações. Segundo as estimativas do banco, o múltiplo de valuation da ação também deve passar por uma reavaliação positiva agora, após o anúncio.

Mesmo com a reavaliação, os analistas ressaltaram que o múltiplo deve continuar sendo pressionado enquanto as investigações permanecerem em andamento. O mesmo vale para a visão do banco sobre a companhia.

Reintegração de Huang

Para o banco, do ponto de vista estratégico, a capacidade de articulação e a influência externa de Huang foram importantes tanto para a Nvidia quanto para o ecossistema mais amplo de inteligência artificial.

Ainda não está claro se a companhia pretende continuar negociando novos investimentos envolvendo múltiplas partes, como acontecia anteriormente, mas o papel do CEO pode voltar a ser crucial neste quesito.

Da mesma maneira, segundo o Goldman, Huang foi fundamental para a cultura corporativa e para os valores que orientam a Nvidia e, com seu retorno, é esperado que a cultura existente da companhia seja reforçada.

Com o andamento das investigações, incluindo a apuração do Departamento de Justiça dos Estados Unidos (DOJ, na sigla em inglês), os analistas acreditam que as operações da Nvidia passem por um nível maior de fiscalização daqui para frente, o que pode ser positivio.

Por outro lado, para o banco, essas mesmas investigações devem continuar pressionando as ações por tempo indeterminado ou, ao menos, enquanto durarem as apurações ou que informações mais detalhadas sejam encontradas.

infomoney_manchetes.titulo: Jensen Huang é reconduzido ao cargo de CEO da Nvidia após crise de espionagem
infomoney_manchetes.resumo: Conselho aprovou por unanimidade a reintegração do executivo e afirmou que decisão não representa risco à segurança nacional dos Estados Unidos
infomoney_manchetes.conteudo_html:
A Nvidia anunciou nesta segunda-feira (23) o retorno de Jensen Huang à presidência executiva da companhia, menos de duas semanas depois de sua saída em meio a uma investigação envolvendo suspeitas de espionagem chinesa. A decisão tem efeito imediato e foi aprovada por unanimidade pelo conselho de administração.

Huang também reassume seu assento no conselho. Segundo comunicado da fabricante de chips, a decisão ocorreu após uma série de conversas com o executivo, nas quais os conselheiros avaliaram sua capacidade de continuar à frente da empresa.

O conselho informou que consultou integrantes do alto escalão do governo dos Estados Unidos antes de autorizar o retorno. Com base nas informações recebidas, a companhia concluiu que a reintegração de Huang não representa ameaça à segurança nacional americana.

Investigação sobre espionagem continua

O retorno de Huang ocorre após sua renúncia, anunciada em 12 de novembro, em meio a revelações sobre sua vida pessoal e possíveis vínculos com uma operação de inteligência estrangeira.

A Nvidia havia iniciado uma investigação independente depois de reportagens indicarem que o executivo poderia ter sido alvo de uma tentativa de obtenção de informações por agentes ligados à China.

A empresa afirmou que o processo de apuração continuará, mesmo com o retorno de Huang.

infomoney_manchetes.titulo: Férias de 30 dias úteis? Projeto quer ampliar descanso dos trabalhadores; entenda
infomoney_manchetes.resumo: Proposta apresentada na Câmara exclui sábados, domingos e feriados da contagem das férias e prevê prazo de adaptação para empresas
infomoney_manchetes.conteudo_html:
Os trabalhadores brasileiros poderão ter direito a um período maior de férias caso avance no Congresso um projeto de lei apresentado pelas deputadas Sâmia Bomfim (PSOL-SP) e Duda Salabert (PSOL-MG). A proposta substitui a contagem atual de 30 dias corridos por 30 dias úteis de descanso remunerado.

Na prática, a mudança ampliaria o período de afastamento do trabalho. Para quem trabalha de segunda a sexta-feira, por exemplo, 30 dias úteis corresponderiam a seis semanas de férias, sem considerar eventuais feriados.

O Projeto de Lei 5.858/2026, apresentado em 16 de novembro, prevê alterar a Consolidação das Leis do Trabalho (CLT) e estender a nova forma de contagem a outras categorias profissionais, como empregados domésticos, aeronautas e atletas profissionais.

Atualmente, a legislação prevê até 30 dias corridos de férias após cada período de 12 meses de trabalho, conforme as regras da CLT. Isso significa que finais de semana e feriados são contabilizados durante o afastamento, independentemente dos dias em que o empregado trabalharia normalmente.

O que mudaria nas férias?

Pelo projeto, o trabalhador passaria a ter 30 dias úteis de descanso. Sábados, domingos e feriados ficariam fora da contagem, prolongando o período total de férias.

Na justificativa, as autoras argumentam que o descanso semanal e os feriados são direitos já assegurados aos trabalhadores e, por isso, deveriam ser contabilizados separadamente das férias anuais.

As deputadas também apontam diferenças entre trabalhadores que saem de férias em épocas distintas do ano. Atualmente, um empregado que tira férias durante um período com vários feriados pode ter menos dias efetivos de descanso em relação a outro que se afasta em um mês sem datas comemorativas.

Quando a nova regra poderia começar a valer?

O texto prevê um período de adaptação de 180 dias após a publicação da eventual lei. A mudança seria aplicada somente aos períodos aquisitivos de férias iniciados depois da entrada em vigor da nova legislação. Assim, férias já adquiridas anteriormente continuariam submetidas às regras atuais.

O prazo de transição foi incluído para permitir que empresas reorganizem escalas de trabalho, substituições temporárias e planejamento de pessoal.

A proposta está em tramitação na Câmara dos Deputados e ainda precisa passar pelo processo legislativo antes de produzir efeitos. Caso seja aprovada pela Câmara e pelo Senado, sem alterações que exijam nova análise, seguirá para sanção presidencial.

medium.titulo: The Handoff Is the Product: Where an AI Agent Should Stop and a Person Should Take Over
medium.resumo: By Shawn Carter, Manager at Autoesta. We build AI agents, CRM systems and automations for service businesses.
medium.conteudo_html:
By Shawn Carter, Manager at Autoesta. We build AI agents, CRM systems and automations for service businesses.

Most of the questions we get about AI agents are about the model. Which one is smartest, which one sounds most human on a call, which one is cheapest per message. Those are fair questions. In our view they are not the ones that decide whether an agent helps a business or embarrasses it.

What decides it is the handoff: the exact moment the agent stops and a person takes over, and what that person receives when they do. We now write the handoff rules before we write a single prompt. This piece explains why, and what those rules look like.

Why the handoff matters more than the model

Picture an agent that handles nine messages in ten well and fumbles the tenth. That tenth message is where the angry customer, the refund, the legal question and the big deal sit. Those are the conversations a business can least afford to fumble.

The research we trust most points the same way. In “Generative AI at Work” (NBER working paper 31161), Brynjolfsson, Li and Raymond studied 5,179 customer support agents who were given an AI assistant in stages. Issues resolved per hour rose about 14 percent on average, and the biggest gains went to newer, less experienced staff. That study measured AI helping people, not AI replacing them. The lesson we take from it is that the best results come from a person and a system working the same conversation, with a clean line between them.

So when a client asks “how much of this can the agent do alone?”, our honest answer is: less than you think at launch, more over time, and only as fast as the handoff earns trust.

The four moments an agent should stop

These are the rules we set on every build, whatever the channel (phone, SMS, WhatsApp, web chat or Instagram DMs).

1. The customer asks for a person. Words like “speak to someone”, “real person”, “complaint” or “refund” end the AI’s turn. We don’t let the agent argue, try once more, or ask “are you sure?”. The cost of a frustrated customer is far higher than the cost of a staff member reading a message.

2. The answer isn’t in the approved content. An agent should answer only from information the business has signed off: services, hours, policies, prices it is allowed to quote. When the question falls outside that, the right reply is “let me get someone who can answer that properly”, not a confident guess. A made-up refund policy or price is the classic agent mistake, and it is completely avoidable.

3. The action is hard to undo. Booking a slot is easy to fix. Sending a message to a whole list, issuing a refund, changing a payment or deleting a record is not. Our rule: the agent can prepare those actions, but a person approves them. Fixed, rule-based steps (invoices, eligibility checks, compliance steps) stay in plain workflows where the same input always gives the same result. The agent handles the parts where the input varies and judgment helps.

4. The lead is hot. This one surprises people. When a lead says they want to buy, book a large job or talk pricing for a big project, the agent’s job is to get a person on the conversation quickly, not to close the deal itself. The agent qualifies, routes and books; people sell the conversations that matter most.

What the person should receive

A handoff that drops the customer into a staff inbox with no context is barely better than no agent at all. The customer has to repeat themselves, and the staff member starts cold.

Every handoff we build passes on four things:

  • A short summary of what the customer wants, in one or two lines.
  • What the agent already said, so the person doesn’t contradict it.
  • The reason for the handoff (asked for a person, outside approved content, risky action, hot lead).
  • The next step the agent promised, such as “someone will call you within the hour”, so the business can keep that promise.

In GoHighLevel this usually means a tag, a note on the contact, an assigned owner and an alert to the right person. In other systems it’s the same idea in different fields. The tools matter less than the rule: the person picks up exactly where the agent left off.

Calling has its own rules

Voice agents need extra care. In February 2024 the FCC ruled that AI-generated voices count as “artificial” voices under the Telephone Consumer Protection Act, so outbound AI calls need the same prior consent as prerecorded calls. That doesn’t make AI calling off limits. It means inbound answering, confirmations and calls to people who asked to hear from you are a very different risk from cold outbound dialling. We treat consent records as part of the build, not an afterthought.

How we decide what to automate first

Our view is simple: start with the jobs where a wrong answer is cheap and a slow answer is expensive.

Missed calls are the best example. One of the businesses we work with, a handyman and property maintenance company, runs a missed-call auto reply so a new customer who calls during a job gets a text back instead of silence. A slightly imperfect text is far better than a voicemail nobody returns until evening. Lead routing is another: a personal training gym we built for gets enquiries from Yelp, Facebook lead ads, Google lead forms, its website and Mindbody, and the system’s first job is making sure each one reaches the right coach.

Neither of those needs an agent to be brilliant. They need it to be fast, polite and clear about when it hands over.

The jobs we push later are the ones where mistakes are costly: quoting complex prices, handling disputes, anything regulated. Those come once the business has seen weeks of real conversations and trusts where the agent’s limits are.

The questions to ask before you buy any AI agent

If you’re comparing AI agent vendors or builders, these questions tell you more than any demo:

  1. What exact words or situations make the agent hand off to a person?
  2. What does my team see when it does?
  3. Which actions can the agent take without approval, and which can’t it take at all?
  4. Where does the agent get its answers, and who approves that content?
  5. How do we measure it after launch (handoff rate, wrong-answer reports, booked appointments)?

A builder who answers these quickly has done this before. One who talks only about the model probably hasn’t thought about that tenth message yet.

Our take

AI agents are worth building for most service businesses we talk to. The value comes from a system that answers instantly, does the repetitive part well, and knows exactly when to step aside. Get the handoff right and the model choice becomes a detail.

If you want to see how we set up qualification and handoff rules, Autoesta publishes how its agents are built, including how its lead qualification agent scores and routes new enquiries (autoesta.com/ai-lead-qualification-agent).

Shawn Carter is a Manager at Autoesta, a 16-person team that builds AI agents, automations and CRM systems for service businesses.

medium.titulo: Cut Your Cloud and AI Bill in 30 Days: A Practical FinOps Checklist
medium.resumo: A week-by-week plan to see every bill, remove waste, pay less for what you keep, and stop surprises.
medium.conteudo_html:
A week-by-week plan to see every bill, remove waste, pay less for what you keep, and stop surprises.

Why small teams overspend on cloud and AI

Most companies with 5 to 200 people have no dedicated FinOps team.

Cloud costs often fall to whoever originally set up the infrastructure, while spending is reviewed only when finance asks why the monthly bill increased. By then, the money has already been spent.

According to Flexera’s 2026 State of the Cloud Report, organizations estimate that 29% of cloud infrastructure and platform spending is wasted.

Three challenges make this especially difficult for smaller teams:

  • Multiple bills: AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, Snowflake, OpenAI and Anthropic costs can appear across separate reporting systems.
  • Rapidly changing AI spending: New product features, coding agents and changes to prompt usage can quickly affect AI costs.
  • Lack of follow-through: Optimization recommendations exist, but they rarely deliver value unless someone owns the changes and verifies the savings.

The following checklist gives founders, engineers and engineering managers a practical 30-day starting point.

Week 1: See every bill in one place

Goal: Establish a clear spending baseline.

Before optimizing costs, understand what you’re spending, where the charges originate and which expenses lack ownership.

Your checklist:

  • List every cloud, data and AI provider you pay.
  • Enable detailed billing exports, including AWS Cost and Usage Reports where applicable.
  • Establish consistent tags or labels such as team, environment and product.
  • Record last month’s total spending and the ten most expensive services.
  • Identify spending without an obvious owner.

What good looks like: By the end of the week, you should be able to explain total spending, its major contributors and the portion that remains unallocated.

CloudQuell provides a consolidated view of supported cloud and AI spending, helping teams establish this baseline without building separate reporting spreadsheets.

Week 2: Remove obvious waste

Goal: Identify unnecessary spending before making larger architectural changes.

Start with resources that may no longer be delivering value.

Where to look for cloud and AI waste

  • Idle compute: Instances or clusters with little activity, including development resources running outside working hours.
  • Oversized compute: Resources with consistently low CPU or memory utilization.
  • Unattached storage: Orphaned volumes, unused snapshots and obsolete backups.
  • Object storage: Data that could be moved to a lower-cost storage class.
  • Networking: Unused load balancers, public IP addresses and unexpected transfer charges.
  • Data warehouses: Compute that remains active when no workload is running.
  • AI APIs: Unused API keys and unnecessarily expensive model choices.

Before deleting or resizing anything, confirm ownership, assess dependencies and record the expected savings.

A lesson from the field

A client had an Amazon EMR cluster left running unnecessarily. It accumulated several thousand dollars in charges while total spending remained within budget.

The example illustrates why staying under budget is not enough to establish that infrastructure is being used efficiently.

Week 3: Pay less for what you keep

Goal: Improve pricing for predictable workloads.

Once unnecessary usage has been addressed, examine the stable portion of your remaining spending.

Cloud providers offer commitment-based discounts, including:

  • AWS: Savings Plans and Reserved Instances.
  • Azure: Reservations and savings plans for compute.
  • Google Cloud: Committed use discounts and eligible sustained use discounts.
  • Snowflake and AI providers: Applicable capacity agreements, batch processing and prompt caching.

The key is to make commitments against a conservative baseline of usage rather than temporary peaks.

Your checklist:

  • Identify the stable usage floor over the previous three months.
  • Evaluate available commitment discounts.
  • Prefer flexible commitment options where workloads are changing.
  • Record commitment expiration dates.
  • Evaluate batching and caching opportunities for suitable AI workloads.

A commitment that expires unnoticed can increase costs even when workload consumption remains unchanged.

Week 4: Put guardrails in place

Goal: Make cost management a repeatable practice.

One-time optimization isn’t sufficient. Teams also need processes for identifying future changes.

Your checklist:

  • Establish monthly budgets by provider and team.
  • Configure alerts at appropriate budget thresholds, such as 80% and 100%.
  • Enable cost anomaly detection to identify unusual spending as billing data arrives.
  • Send a short weekly spending summary to responsible teams.
  • Verify whether Week 2’s optimization changes delivered their expected savings.
  • Assign a named owner for ongoing cloud financial management.

Don’t overlook AI spending

AI services introduce additional cost drivers that deserve attention.

Track spending by provider, model and API key where billing data supports those dimensions.

Beyond total dollars, examine metrics such as cache hit rate and tokens per request. These can help distinguish changes in consumption from changes in workload efficiency.

If your organization uses coding agents, per-developer cost reporting can also help explain adoption and spending.

The 30-day checklist at a glance

Week 1 — See every bill

  • Consolidate cloud and AI billing.
  • Enable detailed exports.
  • Establish consistent tags.
  • Find your highest-cost services.
  • Identify unallocated spending.

Week 2 — Remove waste

  • Review idle and oversized resources.
  • Examine unattached storage.
  • Reduce avoidable network costs.
  • Review data warehouse utilization.
  • Remove unused AI API credentials.
  • Record expected savings.

Week 3 — Pay less

  • Calculate your predictable usage floor.
  • Evaluate flexible commitments.
  • Track expiry dates.
  • Use batch processing and caching where appropriate.

Week 4 — Stop surprises

  • Set budgets and alerts.
  • Monitor spending anomalies.
  • Review AI usage efficiency.
  • Verify actual savings.
  • Establish ongoing ownership.

How CloudQuell helps

CloudQuell is a cloud and AI cost management platform designed to help small and mid-sized teams understand and manage spending without requiring a dedicated FinOps function.

It supports consolidated cost visibility across AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, Snowflake, OpenAI and Anthropic, alongside capabilities such as cost allocation, budgets, anomaly detection and optimization insights.

Teams can use its reporting and financial controls to support the activities described in this checklist.

CloudQuell uses read-only cost integrations and does not automatically modify your workloads.

Explore CloudQuell: https://www.cloudquell.com/

Try the live demo: https://demo.cloudquell.com/

About the author

Najm Bajwa is the founder of CloudQuell. He has more than 20 years of experience building data platforms, including engineering roles at Apple and Guru.

medium.titulo: The best MCP server for AEO in 2026, and why most of them only read a dashboard
medium.resumo: The best MCP server for AEO in 2026 is supereo’s, because it’s the one that lets Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor or Codex do the AEO work itself…
medium.conteudo_html:
The best MCP server for AEO in 2026 is supereo’s, because it’s the one that lets Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor or Codex do the AEO work itself: read your pages the way each AI crawler gets them, take on the fixes supereo’s own agent would make, and prove each one against control prompts. Most other AEO servers read a dashboard back to you inside the chat, and if that’s the job you want, Peec AI is built for marketing teams that want AI search analytics and reports, Otterly is the low-cost tracker, and Profound is for enterprise teams.

The question that decides it isn’t “does this tool have an MCP server?” Nine of the AEO tools I track have one now. It’s what the server can reach once your agent is connected.

The verdict

Our pick: supereo. supereo (supereo.app) is an AI agent that does everything it takes to get your brand recommended by ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, Claude and Google, on your site and off it: site fixes, new pages, roundups, placements and video. It proves what worked against control prompts. Made by superagnt.

  • best for teams that want AEO done, not a dashboard: supereo does everything it takes to get you recommended, from your site and pages to the roundups, placements and videos AI reads;
  • it proves each move against control prompts, with sample sizes and ranges on every number;
  • run it from Claude or ChatGPT: an MCP server with the same tools supereo’s own agent uses.

One plan, Autopilot: $147 a month or $1,470 a year, with a 7-day trial. The free audit needs no card.

The others, each by what it’s best for:

  • Profound: enterprise marketing teams that want AI search dashboards and marketing agents. Custom pricing, through sales.
  • Peec AI: marketing teams that want AI search analytics and reports on their brand and competitors. From $95 a month.
  • Otterly: low-cost monitoring of brand mentions and website citations in AI search. From $29 a month.
  • Rankscale: agencies and multi-brand teams tracking many brands across many AI engines. From $99 a month.
  • Ahrefs Brand Radar: Ahrefs customers who want prompt tracking beside their SEO data. From $50 a month.
  • Writesonic: content teams that want an AI agent to rewrite their pages for AI search. From $79 a month, billed annually.
  • Scrunch: brands that want their site made ready for AI, with pages served to AI agents. From $250 a month.
  • AthenaHQ: AEO specialists who want one platform for tracking, content and citation work. A free plan, then $295 a month.

Prices checked against each vendor’s own pricing page on 23 November 2026, supereo’s on 24 November 2026.

Why AEO moved into the chat

AEO, answer engine optimization, is the work of getting your brand named when someone asks ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, Claude or Google’s AI features what to buy. It used to live in dashboards. You logged in, looked at a chart of mentions, exported a CSV, and then a person went and did something about it, maybe.

MCP (the Model Context Protocol) is the open standard that lets an AI app call outside tools. Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor and Codex all speak it. So the AEO vendors did the obvious thing and put their data behind a server, and now the agent that writes your landing page can also look up how that page is doing, in the same thread.

That’s real progress. It also hides a split that most roundups on this question skip. A server is a list of tools, and the tools decide what your agent can actually do. Some servers let it read. A few let it act. One lets it check whether acting worked.

Three things an AEO server can reach

1. The vendor’s stored data. This is what most AEO servers expose, and their own pages say so plainly. Peec AI’s server connects Claude and ChatGPT “directly to your Peec AI data.” AthenaHQ’s lets an assistant “query your AI search visibility data in plain language.” Scrunch’s lets you “query your brand monitoring data directly inside Claude, ChatGPT” and other assistants. Writesonic’s gives you “answers from the same data the dashboard shows.” Rankscale’s returns “your dashboard’s numbers with the AI answer behind them.” (Each read on the vendor’s MCP page on 4 November 2026, Rankscale’s on 20 November.)

That’s useful. It’s also the answers their schedulers already collected, so your agent is reading a report, not asking a question.

2. The live web. Can the server fetch your page right now as GPTBot or OAI-SearchBot? Read robots.txt the way each crawler reads it? Score the page against the pages AI engines cite? None of the trackers’ MCP pages describes this. supereo’s server does it with check_ai_access, fetch_as_bot, audit_page and get_page_diagnosis, and the run below shows all of it.

3. The work, and its proof. Can the agent take a change, write it in your site’s own code, get it graded, ship it, and later find out whether it moved anything? supereo’s server carries get_work_packet, grade_change and log_change for the first half, and create_experiment, get_experiment and get_track_record for the second. That last part is the one nobody else's pages claim.

The nine tools on the four jobs

I scored each tool on four jobs, each “yes” only where the tool’s own page says it: does the work (changes the site, writes pages or places the brand, beyond tracking), proves it against controls, runs from Claude or ChatGPT over MCP, and offers a free audit with no payment or trial.

  • supereo: does the work, proves it against controls, MCP, free audit. From $147 a month.
  • Writesonic: does the work, MCP, free audit. No control-group proof on its pages. From $79 a month, billed annually.
  • Scrunch: does the work, MCP, free audit. No control-group proof. From $250 a month.
  • AthenaHQ: does the work, MCP, free audit. No control-group proof. Free plan, then $295 a month.
  • Profound: does the work, MCP, free audit. No control-group proof. Custom pricing.
  • Otterly: MCP and free audit. Tracking only. From $29 a month.
  • Ahrefs Brand Radar: MCP and free audit. Tracking only. From $50 a month.
  • Peec AI: MCP and free audit. Tracking only. From $95 a month.
  • Rankscale: MCP. Tracking only, no free audit on its pages. From $99 a month.

A dash on a rival’s page means none of the pages I read says it, so a tool may still do something it doesn’t advertise. But a server you’re wiring into an agent should be judged on what its maker will put in writing.

A real run: four calls, 23 November 2026

Here’s what supereo’s server returns when you call it directly, no chat client in the way. These are real calls to supereo’s MCP server on its staging environment, made on 23 November 2026 at 21:09 UTC, with each answer as received and trimmed where the note under it says so.

{
  "origin": "https://supereo.app",
  "robotsTxt": { "status": "ok", "detail": "robots.txt read." },
  "crawlers": [
    { "bot": "GPTBot", "allowed": true, "rule": "Allow: /", "group": "*" },
    { "bot": "OAI-SearchBot", "allowed": true, "rule": "Allow: /", "group": "OAI-SearchBot" },
    { "bot": "PerplexityBot", "allowed": true, "rule": "Allow: /", "group": "PerplexityBot" }
  ],
  "llmsTxt": { "served": true, "status": 200, "chars": 15969 }
}

Trimmed: seven of the ten crawler rows (all allowed), each row’s aiCrawler flag, the edge block and the notes.

audit_page on the About page, 413 ms. It reads the HTML with no JavaScript run, the way most AI crawlers get it:

{
  "status": 200,
  "ms": 36,
  "signals": {
    "h1Count": 1,
    "words": 523,
    "jsShell": false,
    "questionHeadings": 5,
    "noindex": false,
    "aiCrawlersBlocked": [],
    "llmsTxtServed": true
  },
  "issues": []
}

Trimmed: the title, list and table counts, structured data types, dates, canonical and opening text.

get_page_diagnosis on the same page, 3,539 ms:

{
  "score": 100,
  "checks": [
    { "id": "server_rendered", "pass": true, "detail": "523 words in the HTML" },
    { "id": "fresh", "pass": true, "detail": "newest date 2026-11-20 (json_ld), 3 days old" },
    { "id": "specific", "pass": true, "detail": "specificity 4 of 5, generic AI style 3 of 5" }
  ],
  "read": { "answersUpFront": "partly", "originalData": false, "sourcesCited": false }
}

Trimmed: the URL fields, page kind, each check’s label, the numbers block, the summary and the cost.

get_fix_playbook for a crawler fix, 187 ms, returned the playbook supereo's own engineer follows. The line worth stealing: "This fix never writes a rule for a search engine's crawler (Googlebot, Bingbot and the rest), and never changes the User-agent: * group, which search engines read."

Two things in there I don’t think people talk about enough. The score is 100 and the content read still says the page answers up front only “partly” and cites no sources: a perfect technical score isn’t the same as a page an engine wants to quote, and the server tells you both. And the playbook is the actual rule set, so when your agent writes the robots.txt fix itself, it inherits the guardrail that stops it from wrecking your Google traffic.

Allowed isn’t served

Here’s a question none of the ranking pages answers: when robots.txt lets a crawler in, does it actually get the page? On 19 November 2026 supereo’s server read canva.com. Its robots.txt disallows GPTBot and ClaudeBot ("rule": "Disallow: /", each in its own group) and lets OAI-SearchBot through. Then fetch_as_bot asked for the home page as each of OpenAI's two crawlers:

{ "bot": "GPTBot", "status": 403, "headers": { "cf-mitigated": "challenge", "server": "cloudflare" } }
{ "bot": "OAI-SearchBot", "status": 200, "htmlChars": 512027 }

Trimmed: the user agents, every other header, the HTML and the notes.

That looks deliberate: no training crawler, yes to search. But the same pattern catches the accidental version, where a firewall’s bot rule turns away the search crawler you meant to welcome and robots.txt looks perfectly fine. A tracker’s server can’t see this, because it never fetches your page. One limit to know: these fetches come from supereo’s address, so a site that verifies crawler IPs may answer the real bot differently, and the tool’s own note says so.

How a fix gets proved

This is where I’d spend most of my attention if I were choosing. A page edit and a rise in mentions in the same month prove nothing by themselves. Models update. Competitors publish. Answers drift from one run to the next. Without a comparison, your agent will happily report a win that was weather.

supereo registers a test when it recommends a change. The change aims at 1 to 5 target prompts, read on all 6 engines supereo tracks, against the brand’s other tracked prompts, the ones no change targets. What the change added is a difference in differences: how much the targets moved minus how much the other prompts moved, in recommendations per 100 answers. Grading starts on day 14 and lands by day 60, on a range built so a “Worked” comes up by luck at most 1 in 20. There are four results:

  • Worked: the whole range is above zero, and the estimate is at least +10 recommendations per 100 answers.
  • No change: the whole range is below +10, and it includes zero.
  • Made it worse: the whole range is below zero, and the change is recorded to be put back.
  • Too close to call: anything else by day 60. It says so instead of rounding up.

From the agent, that’s create_experiment before the change goes live, log_change when it ships, get_experiment for the early numbers and then the verdict, and get_track_record for which kinds of fix keep working on your site. A fix that puts something right, like a crawler rule or a wrong fact, ships without a test. In the dataset, no other tool's pages claim this.

Checking AI answers from your agent

Since this is the part most people connecting a server actually want, here’s what supereo’s tools do for it.

start_audit runs the free audit as you: it works out what you sell and who buys it, writes the 20 questions those buyers would ask, and puts them to five engines (ChatGPT, Gemini, Google AI Mode, AI Overviews and Perplexity) in a minute or two. get_audit returns every answer, with who each engine recommended when it wasn't you. Then list_answers and get_cited_pages read them back one answer at a time, cited URLs included, which are the pages you have to beat or get onto.

For one question on demand, ask_engine asks a single engine now and judge_answer reads the reply. On a plan, 30 tracked prompts run on each of the 6 engines three times a week, so each rate comes out of 100 with its 95% range. Here's a prompt that works as a first message:

Use supereo to run the free audit on acme.com. Then show me the questions
where an engine recommended someone else, with the pages it cited.

The options, one by one

1. supereo. Our pick. Best for teams that want AEO done, not a dashboard. Its server carries the tools supereo’s own agent uses: live crawler and page reads, the answers and cited pages, the work packets and grader for a change, and registered tests. Pros: the only tool here whose pages claim all four jobs; its live crawler and page tools are free for anyone signed in. Cons: one plan at $147 a month, so there’s no cheap tracking-only tier, and the tools that ask engines or register tests need that plan.

2. Writesonic. Best for content teams that want an AI agent to rewrite their pages for AI search. Its pages say its agent “rewrites pages for GEO.” Pros: real page work, free AI-readability tools with no login. Cons: no control-group proof on its pages; the $79 Starter is billed annually and tracks ChatGPT, AI Overviews and Gemini.

3. Scrunch. Best for brands that want their site made ready for AI, with pages served to AI agents. Pros: a serious take on serving agents a version of your site; a free brand audit. Cons: $250 a month to start, with 125 prompts on Core; its server queries monitoring data.

4. AthenaHQ. Best for AEO specialists who want one platform for tracking, content and citation work. Pros: a free Essential plan, a Shopify integration for publishing content, unlimited prompts on the $295 Starter. Cons: the jump from free to $295; no control-group proof on its pages.

5. Profound. Best for enterprise marketing teams that want AI search dashboards and marketing agents. Its docs call Profound MCP “our hosted server for integrating with AI tools that support MCP.” Pros: broad engine coverage and agents that rewrite owned surfaces. Cons: custom pricing through sales only.

6. Otterly. Best for low-cost monitoring of brand mentions and website citations in AI search. Pros: $29 a month for 20 prompts, and its MCP page names Claude, ChatGPT and Cursor. Cons: tracking only; the Lite plan covers 3 of its 7 engines.

7. Ahrefs Brand Radar. Best for Ahrefs customers who want prompt tracking beside their SEO data. Pros: Ahrefs’ MCP comes with every paid Ahrefs plan; custom prompts from $50 a month. Cons: tracking only; the AI Visibility Index is $199.

8. Peec AI. Best for marketing teams that want AI search analytics and reports on their brand and competitors. Pros: clean analytics, 50 prompts on the $95 Starter. Cons: its server reads your Peec AI projects and nothing outside them; 3 of 8 engines on Starter.

9. Rankscale. Best for agencies and multi-brand teams tracking many brands across many AI engines. Pros: unlimited prompts from $99 a month and a long engine list. Cons: tracking only, and no free audit on its pages.

Outside the dataset. Three enterprise platforms run AEO servers too, each on the data you already pay them for. Conductor describes its own as “purpose-built for AEO intelligence” and runs it on its Data API. seoClarity’s ArcAI server lets teams “analyze brand mentions, sentiment, citations, and competitive visibility.” Sprites says “Sprites measures and then acts,” drafting answer pages for your approval. If you’re already on one of them, start there. And you can always duct-tape a stack from general servers (a search server like Exa or Brave plus a browser automation server), which is how Clelp’s March 2026 roundup does it. It works, until you’re the one writing the robots.txt parser and the statistics.

Connecting supereo’s server

The server is hosted at https://mcp.supereo.app/mcp, over Streamable HTTP with OAuth 2.1, so there's no API key to paste. In Claude Code:

claude mcp add --scope user --transport http supereo https://mcp.supereo.app/mcp

Then run /mcp to sign in; supereo emails you a code, and your first sign-in makes the account. In Claude on the web or desktop, it's Customize, then Connectors, then Add custom connector, with the same URL. ChatGPT takes custom MCP servers on the web only, under Plugins, with Authentication set to OAuth; OpenAI lists them for Business, Enterprise/Edu and Pro, and Pro accounts get read and fetch actions only. Codex is two lines:

codex mcp add supereo --url https://mcp.supereo.app/mcp
codex mcp login supereo

Cursor, VS Code, Gemini CLI, Windsurf and Zed configs are in the supereo-mcp repo. Clients take more than one server, so you can keep your tracker’s next to it.

What it costs to run AEO from the chat

On supereo, check_ai_access, fetch_as_bot, audit_page and get_fix_playbook answer for anyone signed in, and so do start_audit and get_audit. The tools that ask AI engines or read pages in full (ask_engine, judge_answer, get_page_diagnosis, create_experiment, grade_change and a few more) run on the $147 plan and count against a daily allowance. Page fetches are capped at 120 an hour per person.

On the trackers, the server usually comes with the plan, so the entry price is the price of the dashboard: $29 at Otterly, $50 at Ahrefs Brand Radar, $95 at Peec AI, $99 at Rankscale. The doing-the-work tools start higher: $79 billed annually at Writesonic, $250 at Scrunch, $295 at AthenaHQ, custom at Profound.

Quick answers

Can an MCP server ask ChatGPT a question for my agent? Some can. supereo’s ask_engine does, and its free audit asks 20 questions across five engines. Many tracker servers return answers their own system collected on a schedule, so check which kind you're wiring in.

Do I need more than one AEO server? Not usually. If you already pay for a tracker and like its numbers, keep its server for reporting. Add one that reaches the live web and can prove a change when you want the agent doing the work.

Is supereo’s MCP server free? Its live crawler and page tools and the free audit are. The tools that ask engines, score pages in full or register tests need the plan.

How I compiled this

Every price and prompt cap comes from each vendor’s own pricing page, checked on 23 November 2026 (supereo’s on 24 November 2026), in US dollars a month on monthly billing, or the monthly price of an annual plan where that’s the only price shown. Each “yes” on the four jobs comes from the tool’s own product pages, docs and free tools, read on 23 November 2026; each MCP quote is from the vendor’s MCP page, read on 4 November 2026 (Rankscale’s on 20 November). Conductor, seoClarity, Sprites and Clelp are quoted from their own pages, read on 18 November 2026. I made no hands-on comparison of the rivals’ servers. The runs are real calls to supereo’s staging server on 19 and 23 November 2026, trimmed where marked, with no number changed. The full list, with every rival’s plans and the page each fact came from, is in supereo’s guide to the best MCP servers for AEO.

If you want your agent reading a dashboard, connect your tracker’s server. If you want it doing AEO and proving what worked, supereo’s is the one built for that job: run the free audit on your site first, then connect the server and ask it what to fix.

medium.titulo: From AI Coding Sprawl to AI Coding Governance
medium.resumo: How leaders can preserve visibility, trust, value, and control as AI-assisted development becomes an enterprise capability.
medium.conteudo_html:
How leaders can preserve visibility, trust, value, and control as AI-assisted development becomes an enterprise capability.

AI coding governance is not primarily about controlling developers or standardizing tools. It is about preserving the organization’s ability to see, decide, measure, trust and change the engineering capability that AI is now becoming.

That distinction matters because the weakest governance response to AI-assisted development is also the most tempting one: turn a complex organizational shift into a tool-control problem.

Approve this assistant. Block that extension. Standardize this model. Update the policy. Add a review gate.

Some of that may be necessary. None of it is sufficient.

The deeper question is whether the organization can still understand how software is being produced, who is making material decisions, what value is being created, what data is crossing which boundaries and whether critical dependencies can be changed when conditions change.

If it cannot answer those questions, the issue is no longer AI adoption. It is engineering governance.

Four Problems, One Organizational Question

This series began with tool visibility: AI coding tools can enter the engineering environment through individual accounts, IDE extensions, team experiments and local workflow choices faster than formal technology management can observe them.

It then moved to strategy: an organization can have a formal AI strategy while its actual AI-assisted development strategy is shaped by decentralized choices across teams.

The third question was productivity. Faster coding is not automatically faster engineering. Accepted suggestions are not customer value. If review, testing, integration, architecture or release management remain constrained, AI may accelerate activity without improving throughput.

The fourth question was trust. When AI-assisted development tools process prompts, code snippets, repository context, issue content, telemetry or identity-linked usage data, permission is not understanding.

Each problem appears different. One belongs to IT asset visibility. One to engineering leadership. One to productivity measurement. One to security and data governance.

Together they point to one organizational question: who governs AI-assisted engineering as an enterprise capability?
Why Existing Governance May Not Be Enough
Many organizations already have governance mechanisms that should apply.

Engineering leaders set standards for development practices. Security teams manage data protection, identity, access and risk. IT manages approved tools and enterprise architecture. Procurement and vendor management review suppliers. Legal and compliance assess contractual and regulatory exposure. Finance asks whether investments create measurable value.

AI coding does not invalidate these disciplines.

The risk is different: it cuts across them too quickly and too quietly.

A coding assistant may look like a developer productivity tool to engineering, a SaaS application to IT, a data-processing concern to security, a contract to procurement, a cost line to finance and a strategic capability to the CIO or CTO. Each function may see a valid fragment. None may own the whole operating model.

That is where two gaps need to be separated.

The first is a responsibility gap. The organization may have all the right functions involved, but no shared view of when an engineering workflow becomes a platform dependency, a security exposure, a supplier commitment or a productivity strategy.

The second is a technical capability gap. The organization may not have reliable ways to observe which tools are being used, verify what data is processed, control which configurations apply, or trace how AI-assisted workflows interact with repositories, identities and delivery systems.

Those gaps are related, but they are not the same. Fragmented ownership does not automatically require a new platform. Missing technical visibility does not automatically require a new committee. The first asks who decides. The second asks what the organization can actually see, verify and control.

If the organization has clear tool inventories, enforceable development standards, mature software delivery metrics, strong supplier governance and well-understood data flows, then AI coding governance may not require a new structure. Existing governance may simply need to extend its scope.

But if those mechanisms are fragmented, AI will not create the gap. It will expose it.

This is why the NIST AI Risk Management Framework is useful, but limited in this context. NIST frames AI risk management around functions including Govern, Map, Measure and Manage, emphasizing that AI risk should be addressed through organizational processes, roles and continuous assessment: https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework. That is directly relevant. But NIST does not tell a specific engineering organization how to assign decision rights between platform teams, security, product engineering and executive leadership for AI coding workflows.

Similarly, the DORA research program is valuable because it keeps the conversation anchored in software delivery performance rather than tool enthusiasm. DORA’s research and capabilities work focuses on software delivery performance, reliability and organizational capabilities: https://dora.dev/research/ and https://dora.dev/devops-capabilities/. That helps leaders avoid mistaking local activity for system performance. But DORA does not automatically answer whether a coding assistant should be treated as an engineering platform dependency, a security exposure, a productivity investment or all three.

That is the governance gap: not the absence of frameworks, but the absence of integration.

Governing the Capability, Not the Tool

The most useful mental shift is to stop asking, “Which AI coding tools do we allow?” as the primary question.

A better question is: “What must remain governable as AI becomes part of software engineering?”

I would start with five dimensions. This is my proposed framework, not an industry standard.

First, visibility. The organization needs to know which tools, accounts, extensions, integrations and workflows are actually in use. Not because every experiment requires executive approval, but because invisible dependencies cannot be evaluated, funded, secured, measured or changed.

Second, decision rights. Someone must be able to distinguish between individual experimentation, team convention, platform standard and enterprise commitment. A developer trying a tool is not the same as a team embedding it into delivery practice. A team convention is not the same as an enterprise dependency. Governance should make those thresholds explicit.

Third, value. AI coding cannot be assessed only through adoption rates, suggestion acceptance or subjective enthusiasm. Those signals may matter, but they are not enough. The natural owner here is engineering leadership: CTOs, VPs of Engineering and engineering managers who must connect AI use to flow, quality, maintainability, reliability and business outcomes.

Fourth, trust. The organization needs evidence about what data is processed, where, under which configuration, with which identity and permission model, and under which retention or training conditions. This is where security, privacy, legal and engineering must meet. The goal is not to frighten developers away from useful tools. The goal is to know which trust boundary has actually been crossed.

Fifth, adaptability. A tool can be useful and still create dependency. The question is whether the organization retains the expertise, architectural flexibility, contractual options, auditability and recovery path to change providers or operating models later. In this context, retained control means understanding dependencies, switching options and recovery paths in practical terms.

These five dimensions are a way to prevent AI coding governance from collapsing into either blanket permission or blanket restriction.

The Case for Coordination Without Uniformity

The strongest objection is worth taking seriously: bottom-up technology adoption is often how real innovation happens.

That is true. Many valuable engineering practices spread because practitioners discovered better ways of working before the organization formalized them. Excessive central control can slow learning, reduce ownership and produce compliance theatre instead of better engineering.

The answer is not mandatory uniformity.

The answer is coordinated autonomy.

Consider a hypothetical organization where several product teams independently adopt different AI coding assistants. One team uses AI mainly for test generation. Another uses it for refactoring legacy code. A third uses it inside an IDE connected to internal repositories and issue context. A fourth uses a separate tool for documentation and code explanation.

A poor governance response would be to ban everything until a central committee selects one approved tool.

An equally poor response would be to celebrate experimentation while ignoring the fact that four different workflows may now imply different data flows, identity models, productivity claims, vendor dependencies and support expectations.

A better response would not begin with standardization. It would begin by classifying the decisions already being made.

The key is not an arbitrary numerical threshold. It is a qualitative change in consequence.

Local experimentation starts becoming organizational dependency when a team depends on the tool to meet delivery commitments, when the workflow affects other teams through shared repositories or platform conventions, when enterprise contracts or support expectations are required, or when removing the tool would create meaningful disruption, rework or loss of capability.

Sensitive data access is different. If an experiment involves sensitive code, customer-related context, privileged repository access, identity-linked telemetry or movement across a trust boundary, governance may need to intervene before the workflow becomes operationally dependent. The issue is not whether the tool has become strategic yet. The issue is whether the experiment has already created a security or data exposure the organization must understand.

Those triggers are different in kind from individual exploration. They change the decision from “Can this developer or team try something useful?” to “Has this become part of how the organization produces software?” or “Has this crossed a boundary that requires evidence before it continues?”

At that point, the decision is no longer only local. It needs shared ownership.

This does not eliminate developer autonomy. It protects it from becoming accidental enterprise architecture.

What Should Change in Practice

For CIOs, CTOs, CISOs and VP Engineering leaders, the immediate implication is not to create a large new bureaucracy around AI coding. The immediate implication is to make existing governance conversations more precise.

Engineering leadership should own the productivity question. Not vendor productivity claims. Not generic AI adoption targets. The real question is whether AI improves the engineering system: delivery flow, quality, maintainability, reliability and the ability to change software safely.

Security and privacy leaders should own the trust-boundary question. Not by reducing every discussion to risk avoidance, but by requiring evidence where data, code, prompts, repository context, telemetry or identity-linked usage may leave a local environment or enter a provider-controlled processing environment.

IT and platform leaders should own the dependency question. Which tools are becoming part of the development platform? Which integrations require lifecycle management? Which capabilities would be difficult to replace? Which teams depend on configurations no one else understands?

Procurement and vendor management should own the supplier question. Not merely price and contract duration, but service continuity, data terms, auditability, support, portability and exit conditions.

Executives should own the threshold question.

At what point does local adoption become a strategic commitment?

That threshold is the missing management object in many AI adoption discussions.

Without it, organizations oscillate between enthusiasm and control. Teams experiment; leadership reacts. Security asks for evidence after workflows have already spread. Procurement enters after dependence has formed. Productivity is asserted before the system has been measured. Strategy is declared after practice has already moved elsewhere.

Governance should change the sequence.

Not by slowing every decision, but by making the few consequential transitions visible earlier.

When Existing Governance Is Enough

There are cases where a dedicated AI coding governance capability may be unnecessary.

If an organization already has strong engineering standards, clear platform ownership, mature security review, reliable technology inventories, disciplined vendor management and meaningful software delivery metrics, then AI coding may be governed through existing channels. In that environment, creating a separate governance layer could duplicate controls and confuse accountability.

That is a real risk. Governance can become an organizational reflex: when a topic feels important, create a committee, a policy, a dashboard and a new approval path. The result may be more meetings without better decisions.

The test should be practical.

Can the organization identify which AI coding tools and workflows are in use? Can it distinguish experimentation from dependency? Can it evaluate productivity at the system level? Can it understand data flows and trust boundaries? Can it change providers or practices without unacceptable disruption? Can accountable leaders make these decisions before the choices become irreversible?

If the answer is yes, existing governance may be enough.

If the answer is no, the organization does not need performative AI governance. It needs an integrated capability to govern AI-assisted engineering proportionately and continuously.

From Adoption to Organizational Capability

The broken assumption is that AI coding governance is mainly about deciding which tools developers may use.

The deeper issue is that AI is becoming part of the software engineering operating model. It influences how code is written, reviewed, tested, explained, documented and maintained. It changes the relationship between individual productivity and organizational throughput. It introduces new trust boundaries into daily engineering work. It can create dependencies before leaders recognize them as dependencies.

That does not make AI coding bad. It makes it consequential.

The goal is not to suppress experimentation. The goal is to prevent experimentation from silently becoming architecture, procurement, security posture, productivity strategy and dependency model all at once.

A mature organization should be able to say: we know where AI is being used in engineering; we know which uses are experimental and which are operational; we know what value we are measuring; we know which data and trust boundaries are involved; we know who has decision authority; and we know how we would change course if needed.

That is governance as organizational capability, not governance as control theatre.

The real question is not whether your developers are ready for AI. It is whether your organization is ready to govern the engineering capability that AI is becoming.
