medium.conteudo_html:
How to master engineering fundamentals, develop computational skills, and thrive in the age of artificial intelligence.

Engineering education can be both exciting and overwhelming. From mastering complex mathematical equations to solving challenging technical problems, engineering students are expected to develop a wide range of skills in a relatively short period. But what if there were a smarter, more efficient way to navigate this demanding journey?

Success in engineering is not simply about memorizing hundreds of formulas. It is about understanding fundamental principles, recognizing patterns, and knowing how to apply the right mathematical tools to real-world problems. A strong foundation in mathematics, mechanics, and computational methods can make even the most challenging engineering subjects more approachable.

Modern engineering students also have access to powerful computational tools. MATLAB and Python can simplify numerical calculations, visualize complex systems, analyze experimental data, and solve problems that would otherwise require hours of manual work. Learning these tools early can provide a significant academic and professional advantage.

Artificial intelligence is transforming engineering education even further. When used responsibly, AI-powered tools can help students understand difficult concepts, generate computer code, explore alternative solutions, and improve their problem-solving abilities. The future belongs to engineers who combine fundamental knowledge with modern computational skills and critical thinking.

1. Why Engineering Education Is So Challenging

Engineering is one of the most intellectually demanding fields of study. Students must simultaneously develop mathematical knowledge, scientific understanding, computational proficiency, and practical problem-solving skills.

A typical engineering student encounters subjects such as:

  • Calculus and differential equations
  • Linear algebra
  • Probability and statistics
  • Statics and dynamics
  • Mechanics of materials
  • Fluid mechanics
  • Thermodynamics
  • Numerical analysis
  • Computer programming
  • Engineering design

Each subject introduces new concepts, equations, and methods. More importantly, these subjects are interconnected.

Differential equations appear in heat transfer, structural dynamics, electrical circuits, and fluid mechanics. Linear algebra is essential in structural analysis, finite element methods, machine learning, and robotics.

Recognizing these connections can dramatically simplify the learning process.

Instead of treating every engineering course as an isolated subject, students should begin to see engineering as a unified system of knowledge.

2. Master the Essential Engineering Formulas

Every engineering student needs a reliable collection of fundamental mathematical and scientific equations.

However, memorizing equations without understanding their physical meaning is one of the most common mistakes students make.

Consider Newton’s second law:

F = ma

This simple equation connects force, mass, and acceleration. It forms the foundation of classical dynamics and appears throughout mechanical, civil, and aerospace engineering.

Similarly, the fundamental equation for normal stress is:

σ = F/A

This equation helps engineers understand how forces are distributed over the cross-sectional area of a material.

Hooke’s law provides another essential relationship:

σ = Eε

It connects stress, strain, and the elastic modulus of a material under uniaxial linear elastic conditions.

These equations are relatively simple, yet they form the starting point for sophisticated engineering theories and computational models.

Essential formulas every engineering student should recognize

ConceptFundamental equationNewton’s second lawF = maNormal stressσ = F/AEngineering strainε = ΔL/L₀Hooke’s lawσ = EεKinetic energyKE = ½mv²Gravitational potential energyPE = mghMechanical powerP = W/tFluid pressure at depthp = p₀ + ρghOhm’s lawV = IRSensible heat energyQ = mcΔTNatural frequency of a spring-mass systemωₙ = √(k/m)Euler’s critical buckling loadPcr = π²EI/(KL)²

These equations represent only a small fraction of the mathematical knowledge required in engineering. Nevertheless, they demonstrate how fundamental principles can describe a wide variety of physical phenomena.

Whenever you encounter a new equation, ask yourself:

  • What physical phenomenon does this equation describe?
  • What assumptions were used in its development?
  • What are the units of each variable?
  • Under what conditions is the equation valid?
  • What happens when one of the variables approaches zero or becomes very large?

Understanding these questions is far more valuable than memorizing the equation itself.

A good engineer does not simply know which formula to use. A good engineer knows why that formula works.

3. Develop a Systematic Problem-Solving Method

Many engineering students struggle not because they lack mathematical ability, but because they do not have a systematic approach to solving problems.

A structured problem-solving strategy can significantly improve accuracy, efficiency, and confidence.

The following seven-step method can be applied to most engineering problems:

  1. Read the problem carefully and identify the objective.
  2. List all known quantities and unknown variables.
  3. Draw an appropriate diagram or physical representation.
  4. Identify the governing physical principles.
  5. Select the appropriate mathematical equations.
  6. Perform the calculations using consistent units.
  7. Verify the results and evaluate their physical meaning.

The final step is particularly important.

Suppose your calculations indicate that a small steel beam deflects by several meters under a modest load. Even if your mathematical calculations appear correct, the result should immediately raise questions.

Engineering is not merely about obtaining numerical answers. It is about obtaining answers that make physical sense.

This ability to evaluate results critically becomes increasingly important when using computational software and artificial intelligence.

4. MATLAB: A Powerful Tool for Engineering Students

MATLAB has become one of the most widely recognized computational environments in engineering education and research.

Its strength lies in its ability to perform sophisticated mathematical operations using relatively simple commands.

Engineering students can use MATLAB for:

  • Matrix and vector calculations
  • Solving systems of equations
  • Numerical integration and differentiation
  • Solving differential equations
  • Data analysis and visualization
  • Structural and mechanical simulations
  • Optimization and control systems
  • Finite element analysis

Consider a simple engineering problem involving Hooke’s law.

Suppose a steel specimen has an elastic modulus of 200 GPa. We want to calculate the stress corresponding to different values of strain within an assumed linear elastic range.

The MATLAB commands are remarkably simple:

E = 200e9;
strain = linspace(0,0.001,100);
stress = E*strain;
plot(strain,stress/1e6)
xlabel('Strain')
ylabel('Stress (MPa)')
title('Linear Elastic Stress-Strain Curve')
grid on

With only a few lines of code, we can calculate 100 stress values and generate a graphical representation of the material’s elastic response.

The same approach can be extended to nonlinear material behavior, structural analysis, heat transfer, vibration problems, and other engineering applications.

Why students should learn MATLAB early

Learning MATLAB during the first or second year of an engineering program allows students to apply computational methods throughout their education.

Instead of performing repetitive calculations manually, students can concentrate on understanding physical behavior, investigating mathematical relationships, and exploring alternative solutions.

MATLAB is not a replacement for mathematical understanding. It is a powerful extension of it.

5. Python: The Versatile Programming Language for Modern Engineers

While MATLAB offers a specialized environment for scientific and engineering calculations, Python provides a flexible and widely accessible programming ecosystem.

Python has become particularly important in scientific computing, data science, automation, artificial intelligence, and machine learning.

Several Python libraries are especially valuable for engineers:

Python libraryPrimary applicationNumPyNumerical and matrix calculationsSciPyScientific computing and optimizationMatplotlibGraphical visualizationSymPySymbolic mathematicsPandasData analysisScikit-learnMachine learningPyTorchDeep learningTensorFlowArtificial intelligence

The previous stress-strain example can also be implemented in Python:

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
E = 200e9
strain = np.linspace(0, 0.001, 100)
stress = E * strain
plt.plot(strain, stress / 1e6)
plt.xlabel("Strain")
plt.ylabel("Stress (MPa)")
plt.title("Linear Elastic Stress-Strain Curve")
plt.grid()
plt.show()

The results are essentially identical to those obtained using MATLAB.

However, Python provides additional opportunities for integrating engineering calculations with databases, web applications, machine learning models, and automated workflows.

Another major advantage is that Python and many of its scientific libraries are freely available and open source.

For engineering students who want to develop skills extending beyond traditional engineering applications, Python is an excellent investment of time.

6. MATLAB vs. Python: Which Should Engineering Students Learn?

This question frequently arises among engineering students.

The answer depends largely on the student’s objectives, academic environment, and professional interests.

FeatureMATLABPythonEngineering calculationsExcellentExcellentEase of learning for numerical workHighHighCostGenerally licensedFree and open sourceMatrix operationsBuilt-inAvailable through NumPyScientific visualizationExcellentExcellentEngineering-specific toolboxesExtensiveDistributed across librariesArtificial intelligenceStrongExtensive ecosystemGeneral-purpose programmingMore specializedHighly versatileAcademic engineering applicationsExcellentExcellent

MATLAB is particularly attractive for students studying numerical methods, control systems, structural mechanics, and traditional engineering simulations.

Python is particularly attractive for students interested in automation, data science, machine learning, and interdisciplinary applications.

The ideal approach is to learn both.

Begin with the computational environment most commonly used in your engineering program. Once you understand the fundamental principles of programming and numerical computation, learning a second language becomes considerably easier.

Programming languages may change, but computational thinking remains valuable throughout an engineering career.

7. Artificial Intelligence: The New Engineering Learning Partner

Artificial intelligence is introducing a new dimension to engineering education.

Students can now interact with AI-powered systems that explain mathematical concepts, generate programming examples, identify coding errors, and assist with technical problem-solving.

Tools such as ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and GitHub Copilot can support many aspects of engineering education.

Potential applications include:

  • Explaining difficult mathematical derivations
  • Generating MATLAB and Python scripts
  • Debugging computer programs
  • Creating practice problems and exercises
  • Summarizing technical literature
  • Exploring alternative engineering designs
  • Understanding unfamiliar scientific terminology
  • Preparing for examinations and technical interviews

For example, an engineering student studying beam bending could ask an AI assistant:

Explain the Euler–Bernoulli beam equation using simple physical arguments. Derive the governing equation, explain its assumptions, and provide a numerical example with MATLAB and Python implementations.

Within moments, the student may receive a structured explanation that combines theory, mathematics, and computational applications.

This type of interactive learning can make difficult engineering concepts more accessible.

However, there is an important distinction between using AI to learn and using AI to avoid learning.

8. The Hidden Dangers of Relying Too Heavily on AI

Despite its impressive capabilities, artificial intelligence is not infallible.

AI systems can generate incorrect equations, misleading explanations, nonexistent references, inaccurate numerical results, and computer programs containing subtle errors.

These mistakes can have serious consequences in engineering.

An incorrect calculation in a homework assignment may result in a lower grade. An incorrect calculation in the design of a bridge, aircraft, building, or medical device could have far more serious implications.

Engineering students must therefore develop the ability to independently verify AI-generated information.

Whenever you use AI to solve an engineering problem:

  • Check the mathematical derivation.
  • Verify dimensional consistency.
  • Examine the underlying assumptions.
  • Compare results with established analytical solutions.
  • Test generated computer code.
  • Consult textbooks and reliable technical references.
  • Follow your institution’s academic integrity requirements.

AI should accelerate your thinking, not replace it.

The most successful engineering students will not necessarily be those who use AI the most, but those who use it most intelligently.

9. Combining Mathematics, Programming, and AI

The real power of modern engineering education emerges when mathematics, programming, and artificial intelligence are combined.

Imagine an engineering student investigating the deflection of a simply supported beam subjected to a concentrated load at its center.

Under the assumptions of linear Euler–Bernoulli beam theory, the magnitude of the maximum deflection is:

δmax = PL³/(48EI)

Here:

  • P is the applied concentrated load.
  • L is the beam length.
  • E is the elastic modulus.
  • I is the second moment of area.

The student can first derive the equation using traditional mechanics.

Next, MATLAB or Python can be used to calculate the deflection for different beam lengths, materials, and loading conditions.

Finally, an AI assistant can help explain the sensitivity of the results, suggest additional investigations, or assist in developing a more advanced computational model.

The student might discover that doubling the beam length increases the deflection by a factor of eight when all other parameters remain constant.

This observation provides an important physical insight into structural design.

Such an integrated approach transforms a simple textbook exercise into a meaningful engineering investigation.

Mathematics provides the theoretical foundation. Programming provides computational power. Artificial intelligence provides interactive assistance.

Together, these three elements form a powerful framework for modern engineering education.

10. Develop an Engineering Problem-Solving Mindset

Engineering education is about much more than passing examinations.

It is about developing a particular way of thinking.

Successful engineers learn to:

  • Break complicated problems into manageable components.
  • Identify the most important physical variables.
  • Make reasonable simplifying assumptions.
  • Develop mathematical models.
  • Evaluate alternative solutions.
  • Recognize uncertainty and limitations.
  • Communicate technical findings clearly.
  • Learn continuously throughout their careers.

These abilities cannot be acquired simply by reading textbooks or watching online lectures.

They require practice, experimentation, curiosity, and persistence.

Students should challenge themselves to explore problems beyond the minimum requirements of their courses.

Write a program that solves a familiar homework problem. Investigate how changing a parameter affects the solution. Compare numerical and analytical results. Ask an AI assistant to suggest alternative approaches, and then evaluate those approaches independently.

Over time, these activities help transform passive knowledge into practical engineering expertise.

11. A 30-Day Engineering Survival Plan

Developing new skills does not necessarily require months or years of intensive study.

A carefully structured 30-day learning plan can provide an excellent starting point.

Week 1: Strengthen your mathematical foundations

Review essential engineering mathematics, including calculus, linear algebra, differential equations, and dimensional analysis.

Create a personal engineering formula handbook containing important equations, definitions, assumptions, and applications.

Week 2: Learn MATLAB

Practice basic commands, matrix operations, mathematical functions, plotting, loops, and conditional statements.

Develop small programs that solve problems from your engineering courses.

Week 3: Learn Python

Explore Python fundamentals, NumPy, SciPy, and Matplotlib.

Reproduce several of the engineering programs developed during the previous week using Python.

Week 4: Integrate artificial intelligence

Use AI tools to explore mathematical derivations, debug programs, generate exercises, and investigate practical engineering applications.

Complete a small engineering project that combines mathematical modeling, computational programming, and AI-assisted learning.

By the end of the month, you will have developed an introductory set of skills that can be expanded throughout your academic and professional career.

12. Build Your Own Engineering Survival Toolkit

Every engineering student should develop a personal collection of resources that can be used throughout university and beyond.

An effective engineering survival toolkit might include:

  • A comprehensive collection of engineering formulas and equations
  • A reliable scientific calculator
  • MATLAB and Python programming environments
  • Personal libraries of reusable computer programs
  • Engineering textbooks and reference handbooks
  • AI-powered learning and research tools
  • Technical writing and presentation resources
  • A portfolio of completed engineering projects

Do not underestimate the long-term value of maintaining your own collection of formulas, programs, and technical notes.

A MATLAB script written during your second year of university might become the foundation of a more advanced research program several years later.

A mathematical formula that initially appears insignificant may eventually become central to an important engineering application.

Knowledge accumulates, and well-organized knowledge becomes increasingly powerful over time.

13. The Future Belongs to Adaptable Engineers

Engineering is undergoing a significant technological transformation.

Artificial intelligence, machine learning, digital twins, advanced numerical simulations, robotics, and physics-informed neural networks are changing how engineers analyze, design, and optimize complex systems.

Nevertheless, the fundamental laws of mathematics and physics remain indispensable.

Future engineers will need to understand both classical engineering principles and emerging computational technologies.

They must be comfortable deriving equations, writing computer programs, interpreting numerical results, and evaluating AI-generated recommendations.

The engineers who thrive in this environment will be those who remain curious, adaptable, and committed to lifelong learning.

Learning does not end with graduation. In many respects, graduation marks the beginning of a much larger educational journey.

Three Essential Strategies for Engineering Success

If there are only three lessons to remember from this article, they are these:

  • Master the essential formulas. Build a strong foundation in mathematics, mechanics, and engineering principles. Focus on understanding the physical meaning, assumptions, and limitations of every important equation.
  • Embrace MATLAB and Python. Develop practical computational skills that allow you to automate calculations, visualize physical behavior, analyze data, and solve increasingly sophisticated engineering problems.
  • Use AI as a learning partner. Take advantage of artificial intelligence to accelerate learning, explore new ideas, and improve productivity while maintaining independent thinking, technical accuracy, and professional responsibility.

Final Thoughts

Engineering education does not have to be an endless struggle with complicated equations, demanding assignments, and unfamiliar software.

With the right strategies, mathematical foundations, computational tools, and learning habits, students can transform these challenges into opportunities for intellectual and professional growth.

Traditional engineering knowledge and modern technology should not be viewed as competing approaches. They are complementary elements of a more powerful educational experience.

The objective is not simply to survive engineering school.

It is to emerge from it as a confident, creative, technically competent, and adaptable engineer who is prepared to solve the challenges of an increasingly complex world.

If you were starting your engineering education today, which would you prioritize: mastering traditional engineering formulas, learning computational programming, or developing AI-assisted problem-solving skills?

medium.titulo: How Much Do Agent Skills Really Matter? 8 Tasks, 2 Models, 216 Runs
medium.resumo: Haiku + Skills beat unskilled Sonnet at 72% lower cost, discipline skills fired 0% autonomously, and On-Demand beat Always-On.
medium.conteudo_html:
Haiku + Skills beat unskilled Sonnet at 72% lower cost, discipline skills fired 0% autonomously, and On-Demand beat Always-On.

🇹🇷 Bu yazının Türkçe versiyonunu buradan okuyabilirsiniz.

One of the defining ideas in modern coding agents is Agent Skills (SKILL.md): instead of stuffing every project’s system prompt with thousands of tokens of instructions, you package domain expertise into modular skill folders and let the agent load them only when needed.

It is an elegant architecture. Yet most discussions around Skills rely on vibes rather than controlled evidence:

  • Deliverable quality: Do Skills measurably improve engineering outputs, or are they glorified prompt sugar?
  • Autonomous discovery: When several skills sit in the workspace, do agents actually find and invoke the right one?
  • Agent behavior & workflow shift: Does having a Skill change how the agent works — exploring more carefully before editing with less rework churn — or does it fall back on old habits?
  • Speed, consistency & decisiveness: Do agents reach working solutions faster and more reliably across repetitions (pass^k), or do decisions remain shaky?
  • Delivery mechanism: Is On-Demand loading better than Always-On system-prompt injection?
  • Model leverage: Can a smaller, cheaper model paired with a Skill beat a stronger model without one?
  • Failure modes: And can a Skill ever hurt performance?

To answer those questions rigorously, I built skill-eval and ran 216 isolated Docker runs across Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Claude Haiku 5.5. The full harness, tasks, hidden graders, calibration log, and raw dataset.json are public at github.com/ayhanblt/skill-eval.

Experimental Design: Avoiding Toy Benchmarks and Ceiling Effects

Most agent evals suffer from two silent flaws: tasks are too easy (so baselines score 95%+ and hide any real delta), or grading leaks information about which condition produced an artifact. I structured main-v1 around four safeguards:

8 Multi-File Tasks Across 4 Archetypes

  • Tool Craft (tool_craft): Multi-sheet Wall Street Excel financial model (G1 · xlsx) and dynamic data-driven Remotion video (G2 · remotion-best-practices).
  • Workflow Discipline (workflow_discipline): Multi-module production billing bug isolation (G3 · systematic-debugging) and a 14-rule Decimal pricing engine (G4 · test-driven-development).
  • Production Engineering (production_engineering): PostgreSQL query/index/RLS optimization (G5 · supabase-postgres-best-practices) and a botanical conservatory web app (G6 · frontend-design).
  • Proprietary Docs vs. Skill (proprietary_custom): Custom event schema migration (G7) and release-pipeline gate fix (G8) inside a 24-file internal documentation repo.

4 Experimental Conditions & Distractor Isolation

  • Condition A (Baseline): No skills installed.
  • Condition B (Installed / Self-Discovery): 1 target skill + 5 orthogonal distractor skills installed; the prompt gives zero hints about using any skill.
  • Condition C1 (Explicit Invocation): Same 6 skills installed, and the prompt explicitly tells the agent to invoke the target skill.
  • Condition C2 (Always-On Ablation, 4 tasks): The Skill tool is disabled; top-level SKILL.md text is injected directly into the system prompt at turn 0.

Pre-Freeze Calibration & 3-Layer Blind Scoring

  • 3 rounds of pre-freeze calibration: Before running main-v1, I ran 76 Condition-A calibration runs (v1, v2, v3) to remove prompt leaks and raise task difficulty until unassisted baselines stayed below the 9.0 ceiling. All tasks, skills, and the Docker sandbox image were then SHA-256 locked.
  • 3-layer blind scoring: Deterministic hidden graders (LibreOffice formula recalculation, ffmpeg/ffprobe audio-fade analysis, real PostgreSQL EXPLAIN ANALYZE, Playwright + axe-core WCAG audits, 20-mutant mutation tests), 2-pass position-swapped blind LLM adjudication (jev-1.14.0), and 156 blind human visual ratings (G1, G2, G6).

Total compute across the 216 runs came to $29.24 API-equivalent (509.8 total agent minutes), with 0 infrastructure errors and 0 grader errors (213 completed, plus 2 Haiku turn-budget exhaustions and 1 Haiku timeout on G5).

The Big Picture: Overall Results

Across the four conditions, headline product scores (/10) and ETS pass rates (≥ 7.0 plus all critical gates) landed as follows:

  • Condition A (No Skill, n=64): 8.60 / 10 · 84.4% pass (54/64) · 12/16 pass^k · 98.7s median · $0.143 cost per pass
  • Condition B (Installed / Discovery, n=64): 9.31 / 10 · 95.3% pass (61/64) · 14/16 pass^k · 96.0s median · $0.135 cost per pass
  • Condition C1 (Explicit Skill, n=64): 9.18 / 10 · 90.6% pass (58/64) · 13/16 pass^k · 103.5s median · $0.175 cost per pass
  • Condition C2 (Always-On, 4 tasks, n=24): 9.02 / 10 · 91.7% pass (22/24) · 7/8 pass^k · 114.7s median · $0.143 cost per pass

At first glance, Skills lift average quality by ~+0.6 to +0.7 points. Look one level deeper, though, and that average hides dramatic divergence: task deltas range from +4.43 down to -1.75.

Figure 1 — Mean product scores (/10) across all 8 tasks under Conditions A, B, and C1. Tool craft tasks show massive gains while frontend design (G6) regresses.

Finding 1: Tool Craft Is Where Skills Deliver Massive Leverage

Skills produced their strongest lift on tasks governed by strict, non-obvious tooling conventions rather than raw algorithmic reasoning:

  • G1 · Excel Financial Model (xlsx): All 8 unskilled Condition-A runs failed (0/8, 5.00/10). Both Sonnet and Haiku wrote valid openpyxl formulas, yet 0/8 recalculated cached values via LibreOffice, 0/8 fixed OOXML chart hygiene, and 0/8 applied standard financial styling fills. With the xlsx skill, Condition B jumped to 9.43 (8/8) and C1 to 9.28 (8/8) (+4.43 points).
  • G2 · Remotion Video (remotion-best-practices): Baseline Condition A averaged 8.11 (0/8 avoided CSS transform: strings in favor of individual translate/scale + Easing, only 1/8 used @remotion/media Audio). Condition B rose to 9.35 and C1 reached 9.57 (8/8 on @remotion/media audio fade).
  • G5 · Postgres / RLS Tuning: Baseline A scored 9.15 (7/8), while B and C1 both hit 9.75 (8/8).
Key takeaway: Frontier coding models already know Python and TypeScript. What they routinely miss are tacit operational rituals — “recalculate workbook cached values in LibreOffice before delivery” or “use individual transforms instead of CSS transform strings for Studio editing.” That is exactly where a crisp SKILL.md shines.

Finding 2: The Discovery Gap (H1) — Agents Find Tool Skills, Skip Discipline Skills

In Condition B, agents had 1 target skill alongside 5 orthogonal distractor skills and received zero prompting about skills. Their autonomous choices revealed a striking split:

  • Wrong distractor invocations: 0 / 64. Agents never got confused by unrelated skills.
  • Overall target discovery rate: 39 / 64 (60.9%) (Sonnet 5.5: 65.6%, Haiku 5.5: 56.2%).
  • Tool and internal repo skills: G1-xlsx: 8/8 · G7-event-spec: 8/8 · G8-release-sop: 7/8 · G2-remotion: 6/8 · G5-postgres: 6/8 · G6-frontend: 4/8.
  • Process and discipline skills: G3-systematic-debugging: 0/8 · G4-tdd-feature: 0/8.

Figure 2 — Autonomous target skill invocations out of 8 runs in Condition B. Agents reliably discover tooling and proprietary repo skills, yet completely ignore debugging (G3) and TDD (G4) discipline skills.

Agents reach for a Skill when a task names an unfamiliar format or domain (“build an Excel model”, “render a Remotion video”). When asked to “debug a service” or “implement a feature”, they assume they already know how and never open workflow-discipline skills. Even in Condition C1 — where the prompt explicitly asked to invoke the skill — agents only invoked test-driven-development 1/8 times on G4, and tdd_red_before_green stayed 0/8 across every condition.

Finding 3: On-Demand (C1) Beats Always-On Injection (C2) Across Every Metric (H4)

To test whether loading skill text via the Skill tool (C1) outperforms pre-loading the exact same SKILL.md into the system prompt (C2), we ran a matched 4-task ablation (G2, G3, G5, G7). On-Demand C1 (n=32) beat Always-On C2 (n=24) cleanly:

  • Quality & Pass Rate: C1 scored 9.58 (32/32 = 100% pass) vs. C2 9.02 (22/24 = 91.7% pass) (C2 suffered 1 Haiku timeout and 1 Haiku budget exhaustion on G5).
  • Rule Adherence: C1 87.5% vs. C2 84.4%.
  • Speed & Context Tokens: C1 finished faster (99.7s vs. 114.7s median) while using ~12% fewer context tokens (572K vs. 653K mean input+cache tokens).

Why? Beyond avoiding upfront context bloat, C1 also unlocks progressive disclosure. On G2-remotion-display, C2 injected only the top-level SKILL.md, whereas C1 let agents browse supporting rules/*.md reference files inside the skill folder. On the Studio-editable transform & easing check, C1 passed 6/8 while C2 scored 0/6.

Figure 3 — Matched comparison on the 4 ablation tasks (G2, G3, G5, G7). On-Demand C1 outperforms Always-On C2 in quality, pass rate, adherence, latency, and token efficiency.

Finding 4: Haiku + Skill Outperforms Unskilled Sonnet at ~72% Lower Cost (H5)

For teams optimizing inference budgets, the model-leverage result was unmistakable:

  • Haiku 5.5 + Skill (Condition B): 9.34 / 10 · 96.9% pass (31/32) · $0.052 mean API-equivalent cost per run
  • Sonnet 5.5 (Condition A · No Skill): 8.72 / 10 · 84.4% pass (27/32) · $0.185 mean API-equivalent cost per run

Paired with an installed Skill, Haiku 5.5 beat unskilled Sonnet 5.5 by +0.62 points and +12.5 percentage points in pass rate—at roughly 72% lower cost.

Figure 4 — Cost-quality Pareto frontier and pass rates across all 8 tasks (n=32 runs per model×condition cell).

Finding 5: The Honest Negative Result — Why frontend-design Regressed (G6)

The most important cautionary finding came from G6 · Frontend Design:

  • Condition A (No Skill): 8.22 / 10 · 7/8 pass
  • Condition B (Installed): 7.90 / 10 · 6/8 pass
  • Condition C1 (Explicit Invocation): 6.48 / 10 · 3/8 pass (-1.75 points!)

Inspecting the hidden Playwright and axe-core grader logs showed why: frontend-design pushes models toward bold, bespoke layouts, custom typography, and non-template aesthetics. As agents stretched to satisfy that creative ambition in C1, functional reliability cracked—comparison modal & pass-estimator checks dropped from 7/8 (A) to 5/8 (C1), and WCAG contrast checks dropped from 8/8 (A) to 6/8 (C1).

Lesson: Aesthetic Skills can act as a double-edged sword. Unless paired with automated E2E and accessibility gates, nudging an agent to “avoid generic UI and be distinctive” increases the risk of shipping visually ambitious but functionally broken interfaces.

Figure 5 — Left: Deterministic tool-craft check pass counts surging from 0/8 to 7–8/8 on G1 and G2. Right: G6 modal and WCAG contrast pass rates dropping under explicit frontend-design guidance.

Proprietary Docs vs. Skill (G7, G8) & Process Discipline (H3)

  • Docs vs. Skill (G7, G8): When given a well-structured 24-file internal documentation tree, unassisted agents already achieved 9.81–9.95 accuracy. Here, Skills helped primarily with speed rather than correctness (G7 median time dropped from 67.6s in A to 57.6s in C1; G8 dropped from 77.8s to 59.6s).
  • Behavior, Speed & Decisiveness (H3): Access to Skills increased pre-edit exploration (3.9 → 4.8 / 4.9 read steps before first edit), trimmed rework churn (0.23 → 0.20), and boosted post-edit self-verification (81.2% → 87.5%). Overall median latency improved slightly (98.7s in A to 96.0s in B), while consistency (pass^k) jumped from 12/16 (84.4%) to 14/16 (95.3%). Decisiveness split sharply by domain: tool-craft rituals shifted decisively from 0/8 to 8/8 (G1/G2), whereas ingrained coding reflexes—inner-layer defense-in-depth (G3: 0/8) and Red-first TDD (G4: 0/8)—resisted across every condition.

Honest Limitations

To keep these findings properly scoped:

  1. G4 ceiling & TDD resistance: G4 product scores hit 9.96–9.99 across A/B/C1, and the TDD skill was only invoked 1/8 times even in C1. Our evidence speaks to skill-invocation resistance rather than TDD’s effect on correctness.
  2. Clean internal docs (G7/G8): Our 24-file proprietary docs repo was relatively well-organized; messier real-world documentation would likely amplify the Skill advantage.
  3. Sample size & single blind rater: Each task×model×condition cell had n=4 repetitions (n=3 in C2), and all 156 visual rubric items were scored by a single blinded human evaluator (no inter-rater reliability check).

5 Takeaways for Developer Teams

  1. Invest in tool_craft Skills first: Document/asset pipelines, specialized SDK conventions, and database tuning rules deliver the highest ROI (+1.2 to +4.4 points).
  2. Don’t expect agents to auto-trigger workflow-discipline Skills: Debugging and TDD skills saw 0/8 autonomous invocations in Condition B. Use explicit triggers, hooks, or slash workflows for process enforcement.
  3. Prefer On-Demand Skills (C1) over Always-On prompts (C2): Progressive disclosure saves tokens, finishes faster, and unlocks sub-files without cluttering the base context.
  4. Use Skills as a model-downgrade lever: Haiku + Skill beat unskilled Sonnet at ~72% lower API-equivalent cost.
  5. Pair aesthetic Skills with hard verification gates: Whenever a Skill encourages creative freedom (frontend-design), backstop it with E2E assertions and automated accessibility audits.

Technical Environment & Reproducibility

  • Agent Runtime & Models: Every run executed via pinned Claude Code CLI 2.1.330 with medium effort, a 45-turn cap, --strict-mcp-config, --no-session-persistence, and dontAsk permission mode across claude-sonnet-5-5 and claude-haiku-5-5.
  • Isolated Docker Sandbox: Each run executed inside a dedicated node:22-bookworm-slim Docker image (skilleval-sandbox:latest, non-root runner user) with a fresh workspace copy and an ephemeral per-run config directory, guaranteeing zero cross-run state or session leakage.
  • Offline Verification Stack: The container pre-baked pinned Python (openpyxl 3.1.5, pytest 8.3.4, psycopg2-binary 2.9.10, defusedxml) and Node packages (remotion 4.0.545, playwright 1.49.1, axe-core 4.10.2) alongside PostgreSQL, LibreOffice Calc, poppler-utils, ffmpeg, and headless Chromium.
  • Condition Enforcement & Telemetry: Tool calls and edit/verify order were captured via PreToolUse / PostToolUse hooks (hook-events.jsonl) and stream-json transcripts; the Skill tool was explicitly blocked in Conditions A and C2.
  • Blind Adjudication Stack: Code rubric items were evaluated in 2 position-swapped passes by jev-1.14.0, while G1, G2, and G6 deliverables underwent 156 anonymized human visual ratings with model, condition, and cost stripped.
  • Cryptographic Study Lock: Prior to execution, all tasks, skills, rubrics, Docker image digest, and random seed (20261205) were sealed across 599 SHA-256-hashed files in freeze.lock.json, orchestrated by the Python + uv skilleval harness.

All code, task packages, graders, calibration logs, and the full 216-run dataset.json are open-source and reproducible at: 👉

medium.titulo: 不用 Module Federation：用 Web Components 讓 React 和 Vue 元件在同一頁共存
medium.resumo: 作者：廖哲皓（Howard Liao）｜Frontend Lead（Principal Engineer）
medium.conteudo_html:
作者：廖哲皓（Howard Liao）｜Frontend Lead（Principal Engineer）

我是廖哲皓，從事前端開發 14 年以上。帶團隊時常遇到一種情況：有的團隊寫 React，有的寫 Vue，大家各自做好的元件，卻很難放進同一個頁面裡一起用。

這篇分享我做的一個小型微前端示範：在 Vue 3 的主程式裡，同時載入 React 寫的圖表和 Vue 寫的表格。完整程式碼放在 GitHub：https://github.com/necpoctt/micro-frontend-demo

微前端想解決什麼問題？

  • 不同團隊、不同框架，可以各自開發、各自部署
  • 舊系統可以逐步替換，不必一次全部重寫
  • 共用元件不會被綁死在某一個框架上

常見的做法有 Module Federation、single-spa、qiankun 等。這些方案功能完整，但設定和學習成本也比較高。如果需求只是「把幾個元件嵌進另一個框架的頁面」，Web Components 是更輕量的選擇。

架構

專案分成三個部分：

  • react-chart-lib：React 19 + ECharts 做的用電圖表和圓餅圖
  • vue-table-lib：Vue 3 + Ant Design Vue 做的車輛管理表格
  • host-app：Vue 3 主程式，把上面兩個元件組成一個儀表板

兩個元件庫都用 Vite 的 library mode 打包成單一 JS 檔。主程式只要用 script 標籤載入，就能像一般 HTML 標籤一樣使用這些元件。

Vue 元件轉成 Web Component

Vue 內建 defineCustomElement，幾行就能完成：

import { defineCustomElement } from 'vue';
import TableCe from './components/Table.ce.vue';
customElements.define('remote-vue-table', defineCustomElement(TableCe));

元件檔名用 .ce.vue 結尾，Vue 會把元件的樣式一起放進 Shadow DOM。

React 元件轉成 Web Component

React 沒有內建這個功能，所以我寫了一個小工具函式：建立一個繼承 HTMLElement 的類別，在 Shadow DOM 裡用 createRoot 掛載 React 元件；屬性改變時，在 attributeChangedCallback 裡重新 render。

class Wrapper extends HTMLElement {
  static get observedAttributes() { return attributes; }
  constructor() {
    super();
    const mount = document.createElement('div');
    this.attachShadow({ mode: 'open' }).appendChild(mount);
    this.root = ReactDOM.createRoot(mount);
  }
  connectedCallback() { this.render(); }
  attributeChangedCallback() { this.render(); }
}

同一個函式可以註冊多個 React 元件，例如 remote-electricity-chart 和 remote-pie-chart。

主程式怎麼使用

在 host-app 的 index.html 載入兩個打包好的檔案，接著就能在 Vue 範本裡直接使用：

<remote-vue-table
  :table-data="JSON.stringify(tableData)"
  @row-action="handleRowAction">
</remote-vue-table>

另外要在 vite.config.ts 裡設定 isCustomElement，告訴 Vue 編譯器 remote- 開頭的標籤是自訂元素，不要當成 Vue 元件解析。

實作時要注意的四件事

  1. 屬性只能傳字串：物件和陣列要先 JSON.stringify，元件內再 JSON.parse。資料量大或更新頻繁時，可以改用 DOM property 傳遞。
  2. 事件用 CustomEvent：元件把資料放在 event.detail，主程式用一般的事件監聽接收。
  3. 樣式隔離：Shadow DOM 讓元件樣式不會互相污染，但主程式的全域樣式也進不去，主題色要透過 CSS 變數或屬性傳入。
  4. 打包體積：每個元件庫都包含自己的框架（React 或 Vue），檔案會變大。元件少時沒問題；元件多、頁面多時，就該考慮用 Module Federation 共用相依套件。

什麼時候適合這個做法？

適合：

  • 想在既有系統裡逐步導入新框架
  • 跨團隊共用少數幾個元件
  • 讓沒有使用前端框架的頁面（例如後端產生的 HTML）也能使用元件

不適合：

  • 整個產品要拆成很多個獨立部署的子應用
  • 元件之間需要大量共享狀態

微前端不一定要很複雜。先從最小可行的方式開始，真的遇到規模問題再升級架構，通常是比較穩的做法。

medium.resumo: 我是廖哲皓（Howard Liao），寫前端 14 年以上，從 jQuery 時代一路用過 Angular、Vue、React。身為 Frontend Lead，幫專案選框架是我常要做的決定。這篇不比較誰「比較好」，而是分享我做技術選型時實際會考慮的事情。
medium.conteudo_html:
我是廖哲皓（Howard Liao），寫前端 14 年以上，從 jQuery 時代一路用過 Angular、Vue、React。身為 Frontend Lead，幫專案選框架是我常要做的決定。這篇不比較誰「比較好」，而是分享我做技術選型時實際會考慮的事情。

先講結論：框架很少是專案成敗的關鍵

三個框架都很成熟，都能做出好產品。真正影響專案的通常是：團隊熟不熟、架構和規範有沒有建立好、測試和 CI/CD 有沒有到位。所以選框架時，我會先看「人」和「專案」，再看技術本身。

問題一：團隊現在會什麼？

如果團隊大多熟 Vue，硬換 React 的學習成本和初期品質下降，往往比框架本身的差異更大。熟悉度是最被低估的因素。

問題二：專案規模和壽命？

大型、長期、多人協作的企業系統，Angular 內建的結構（DI、模組、TypeScript 優先）能減少「每個人寫法都不一樣」的問題。中小型、需要快速開發的專案，Vue 上手快、模板直覺，新人容易加入。需要高度彈性、大量客製化的產品，React 的套件與社群資源最多。

問題三：招募容易嗎？

在台灣，React 與 Vue 的人才都不少，Angular 相對少一些。如果團隊還要擴編，這點要列入考量。

問題四：有沒有既有系統要整合？

舊系統如果是 jQuery 或 server-side render，要考慮能不能漸進式導入。Vue 在這方面特別友善，可以先從單一頁面開始替換。

問題五：TypeScript 支援？

現在三者對 TypeScript 的支援都很好，我建議新專案一律用 TypeScript，對團隊協作和長期維護的幫助非常大。

選完之後，更重要的事

不管選哪個框架，我都會在專案初期建立：資料夾結構與命名規範、狀態管理原則（什麼放全域，什麼放元件內）、共用元件庫（Material UI 或自建 design system），以及 Lint、格式化、測試、CI/CD。這些基礎打好，換框架反而沒那麼可怕；沒打好，用哪個框架都會越寫越亂。

技術選型沒有標準答案，但有好的思考方式。歡迎分享你們團隊的經驗。

corrida_no_ar.titulo: Disputas ACIRRADAS, resultados e POLÊMICAS pelo BRASIL
corrida_no_ar.resumo: Notícias sobre a chegada emocionante da Maratona de Maringá, a falta de água em Brasília, a invasão de carro em Sorocaba, resultados da Corrida Marco Zero e os problemas relatados na Uphill do Corcovado.
corrida_no_ar.conteudo_html:
Terça-feira | 24 de novembro de 2026

O fim de semana foi marcado pela Maratona de Maringá, que contou com transmissão ao vivo do Corrida no Ar em mais uma parceria com Geraldo Prota, do Runners Hub. A cada transmissão, a equipe tem buscado inovações, como a inclusão de diversos convidados que enriqueceram a cobertura, incluindo o prefeito da cidade, Silvio Barros, e a lenda do atletismo, Vanderlei Cordeiro de Lima. Durante a live, o prefeito revelou com exclusividade a medalha da edição de 50 anos da Prova Tiradentes, que acontecerá em 21 de abril do próximo ano. A prova foi um sucesso, com uma disputa espetacular na chegada masculina. O etíope Adugna Gadisa venceu com o tempo de 2:18:57, apenas um segundo à frente de Jonathan Akankwasa, de Uganda. Entre os brasileiros, o destaque foi José Márcio Leão, em terceiro com 2:21:49, seguido por Gilberto Silvestre Lopes (2:23:23) e Franck Caldeira (2:24:01). No feminino, a etíope Zewdinesh Hursa venceu com 2:43:50, mas a brasileira Glaucielle de Oliveira fez uma estreia impressionante na distância, terminando em segundo lugar com 2:44:30. Apesar do sucesso, o evento recebeu críticas pela longa fila na entrega de kits na sexta-feira e por um erro de percurso nos 10 km, onde os corredores acabaram fazendo 12 km. Ao todo, a maratona teve 888 concluintes, e o evento completo somou 6.935 participantes.

Maratona Monumental de Brasília e a volta da falta d’água

A Maratona Monumental de Brasília, que faz parte do circuito Mega Finish, também aconteceu no domingo. O grande vencedor foi Jonathas de Oliveira, com o tempo de 2:26:00. No feminino, a vitória ficou com a experiente Marily dos Santos, que completou a prova em 3:11:23. Infelizmente, o evento reviveu uma antiga tradição negativa: a falta de água. Após uma edição bem-sucedida no ano passado, a prova voltou a registrar problemas de hidratação, com relatos de falta de água no km 37,5 e até mesmo na linha de chegada para alguns corredores. Essa é uma falha grave que coloca a saúde dos atletas em risco. A maratona contou com 1.474 homens e 362 mulheres, totalizando 1.836 concluintes. Somando todas as distâncias, o evento reuniu 8.836 corredores.

Irresponsabilidade e perigo na Maratona de Sorocaba

A Maratona de Sorocaba foi palco de um incidente grave e lamentável. Um casal visivelmente embriagado invadiu o percurso com um carro, dirigindo de forma perigosa e colocando a vida dos corredores em risco. Após um corredor jogar água dentro do veículo para tentar pará-los, os ocupantes desceram e agrediram o atleta com uma garrafa de cerveja. Outros corredores intervieram, e a situação só foi controlada com a chegada da polícia, que levou o casal para a delegacia. Felizmente, não houve uma tragédia, mas o episódio é um alerta sobre a irresponsabilidade de pessoas que bebem e dirigem. Em relação à prova, o vencedor masculino foi Arnaldo Gonçalves da Silva Neto, com 2:37:11, enquanto Giovanna Battaglin Espigares venceu no feminino com 3:06:35.

Resultados fortes na Corrida Marco Zero em Rondônia

Em Ji-Paraná, Rondônia, a Corrida Marco Zero teve uma disputa de altíssimo nível. A prova de 10 km, conhecida por ser muito rápida, foi vencida por Giovani dos Santos com o excelente tempo de 29:49. Ele ultrapassou Wilson Mutai Maira na metade da prova para garantir a vitória. Maira ficou em segundo com 29:55, seguido por Vitor Ferreira (30:26). No feminino, a disputa foi decidida no sprint final, com Núbia de Oliveira levando a melhor com 35:49, apenas três segundos à frente de Amanda Aparecida de Oliveira (35:52).

Decepção na Uphill Cristo Redentor

A Uphill Cristo Redentor gerou muita frustração entre os participantes. A prova de 18 km foi encurtada para 6,5 km, uma informação que muitos corredores só descobriram na retirada do kit, na sexta-feira, devido a uma obra no percurso. Além disso, a largada atrasou, as marcações de quilometragem estavam confusas e, no final, os atletas receberam apenas uma banana. A principal queixa, no entanto, foi sobre o retorno do Cristo. A promessa de uma descida festiva no trem do Corcovado se transformou em um transtorno, com filas enormes e apenas um trem funcionando, fazendo com que muitos esperassem por horas. A situação gerou uma grande decepção, especialmente para um evento com inscrições caras e que atrai pessoas de vários estados.
